name: Colorado
hero_tagline: Fourteeners, red rock, and the highest paved road in America
hero_description: Four national parks packed into one state — snow-capped peaks in the north, cliff dwellings and canyons in the south, and a whole lot of alpine tundra above 12,000 feet in between.
best_time_to_visit: June through September for the high country — Trail Ridge Road and the Beartooth-style alpine passes are typically snow-free only in this window. Ski season runs roughly December to April.
altitude_or_climate_note: Denver sits at 5,280 ft and many trailheads start above 8,000 ft — give yourself a day to acclimatize before a serious hike, and know the signs of altitude sickness. Mountain weather turns fast: afternoon thunderstorms are a real risk above treeline in summer, so plan high-elevation hikes for early morning.
permits_note: Rocky Mountain National Park requires a timed-entry permit late May–mid October. Maroon Bells requires a reservation or early-morning shuttle in high season. Arches-style timed entry doesn't apply here, but book Black Canyon and Great Sand Dunes camping ahead in summer.
gear_note: Layers regardless of season — it can snow at altitude in July. A high-clearance 4WD vehicle opens up several of the hidden gems below (marked); a regular sedan is fine for everything else.

places.name: Trail Ridge Road
places.description: The highest continuous paved highway in the US, cresting over 12,000 ft through Rocky Mountain National Park. Crosses the Continental Divide with wide-open alpine tundra views and regular elk and marmot sightings.
places.tip: Open roughly late May–mid October, weather permitting. Go early morning for wildlife and to beat the afternoon storm risk.

places.name: Million Dollar Highway (San Juan Skyway)
places.description: The stretch of US-550 between Ouray and Silverton — sheer cliff drops, mining-era switchbacks, and some of the most dramatic mountain scenery of any road in the country.
places.tip: No guardrails on some sections; not for anyone uneasy with exposure. Pairs well with a stop in both historic mining towns.

places.name: Independence Pass
places.description: Climbs to 12,095 ft between Aspen and Twin Lakes with tight switchbacks, alpine meadows, and sweeping views at nearly every turn.
places.tip: Closes in winter; even in July, pack a jacket for the windy, cold summit.

places.name: Maroon Bells
places.description: The most photographed peaks in Colorado, reflected in Maroon Lake — genuinely postcard-worthy, with trails ranging from a flat lakeside stroll to the serious Four Pass Loop.
places.tip: Requires a reservation or early shuttle in season (roughly May–October) — walk-up parking is not realistic in summer.

places.name: Peak to Peak Scenic Byway
places.description: An hour from Denver, threading pine forest and historic mining towns like Nederland with long views of the Continental Divide.
places.tip: Wildflowers in spring/summer, fired-up aspen color in fall — either season works.

places.name: Zirkel Circle Trail
places.description: An 11-mile loop near Steamboat Springs through the Zirkel Wilderness, passing Gilpin Lake with views of Medicine Bow Peak.
places.tip: A full-day undertaking — start early.

places.name: Rocky Mountain National Park
places.description: Colorado's most-visited attraction at over 4 million visitors a year — alpine lakes, waterfalls, elk and marmots, and Trail Ridge Road running straight through it.
places.tip: Book the timed-entry permit well ahead for late May–mid October visits.

places.name: Garden of the Gods
places.description: Dramatic red sandstone rock formations in a free city park, with easy paved paths and dramatic Pikes Peak backdrops.
places.tip: Free and open year-round; go at sunrise or sunset for the best light on the red rock.

places.name: Pikes Peak
places.description: America's Mountain — over 14,000 ft, reachable by the historic Cog Railway or the Pikes Peak Highway, with a visitor center at the summit.
places.tip: Altitude hits fast at the top; take it slow and stay hydrated even if you drove up.

places.name: Mesa Verde National Park
places.description: Preserved Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings, including the famous Cliff Palace — a genuine must for history-minded visitors.
places.tip: Cliff Palace and Balcony House tours are seasonal and ticketed — check ahead.

places.name: Great Sand Dunes National Park
places.description: North America's tallest sand dunes (about 750 ft), incongruously set against the Rocky Mountains in the San Luis Valley.
places.tip: Sand gets very hot in summer afternoons — the surface can burn bare feet by midday.

places.name: Royal Gorge Bridge & Park
places.description: A suspension bridge towering 955 ft over the Arkansas River, with a whole park of activities built around the gorge itself.
places.tip: An hour from Colorado Springs — easy half-day add-on.

places.name: Crystal Mill & Crystal ghost town
places.description: An iconic 1892 wooden mill perched over a waterfall, reached via a rough road past the fading 19th-century mining town of Crystal.
places.tip: The road demands a high-clearance 4WD vehicle — this is not a sedan trip.

places.name: Paint Mines Interpretive Park
places.description: Otherworldly clay formations and hoodoos in shades of orange and white, used historically by Native Americans for pigment — free, and still under most visitors' radar.
places.tip: Best light for photos is early morning or golden hour.

places.name: Black Canyon of the Gunnison
places.description: The most obscure of Colorado's national parks — sheer, dark canyon walls including the 2,250-ft Painted Wall, and a certified Dark Sky Park for stargazing.
places.tip: Most visitors only drive the South Rim; budget at least half a day.

places.name: St Elmo ghost town
places.description: A well-preserved 19th-century mining ghost town near Buena Vista, with original buildings still standing.
places.tip: Combine with a stay in Buena Vista or Salida for food and breweries afterward.

places.name: Castlewood Canyon ruins
places.description: A short, easy hike to the crumbling stone remains of a dam that failed catastrophically in 1933 — an under-visited state park less than an hour from Denver.
places.tip: Good option if you only have half a day near Denver and want something beyond the obvious.

places.name: Golden Gate Canyon State Park
places.description: Panoramic mountain views within an hour of Denver, with far fewer crowds than Rocky Mountain National Park.
places.tip: A good sunrise or sunset stop if you're based in Denver and short on time.

places.name: Rocky Mountain oysters
places.description: Deep-fried bull testicles, originally cooked by ranchers and still a bold, unmistakably Western rodeo-circuit staple.

places.name: Green chile
places.description: A smoky-hot green chile sauce that goes on everything from fries to burritos — Pueblo chile is the local point of pride.

places.name: Colorado lamb
places.description: The state is a top US lamb producer; look for it grilled or in stews, paired with fresh herbs.

places.name: Palisade Peaches
places.description: Grown on the Western Slope, sweet enough to headline the annual Palisade Peach Festival in late summer.

places.name: Craft beer culture
places.description: Over 400 breweries statewide; Denver hosts the Great American Beer Festival, one of the largest beer events in the country.

places.name: Boulder Dushanbe Teahouse
places.description: A hand-carved teahouse gifted by Boulder's sister city Tajikistan, serving traditional chai — an unexpected cultural landmark.

name: Utah
hero_tagline: The Mighty Five, and a desert full of things the parks don't tell you about
hero_description: Five national parks — Zion, Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef, Canyonlands, and Arches — packed into one state's worth of red rock, slot canyons, and hoodoos, plus Moab's world-class off-road and mountain biking terrain.
best_time_to_visit: Shoulder seasons — April-May and September-October — for mild temperatures and thinner crowds. Fall is increasingly called Utah's 'secret season.' Summer daytime heat in the desert parks is intense (100°F+ is common).
altitude_or_climate_note: Desert conditions: carry more water than feels necessary, and know that flash flooding is a real risk in slot canyons after any rain, even distant rain — check forecasts before entering any canyon.
permits_note: Zion's Angels Landing requires a permit lottery (apply well ahead). Arches lifted its timed-entry requirement for 2026, but confirm the current year's rules before you go since this has changed before. Capitol Reef's Fruita Campground requires reservations March-October.
gear_note: A high-clearance 4WD vehicle opens up Cathedral Valley, Hole-in-the-Rock Road, and most of the hidden gems below — a regular car is fine for all five main parks. Water shoes are worth packing for Kanarraville Falls and other wet slot-canyon hikes.

places.name: Highway 12 Scenic Byway
places.description: A roughly 2.5-hour drive through Red Canyon, Bryce Canyon, Grand Staircase-Escalante, and Capitol Reef — one road, four distinct landscapes, with enough pullouts and side trails to make it a full day.
places.tip: Don't rush it — the point is the stops, not the drive time.

places.name: The Narrows
places.description: Zion's signature hike: wading directly up the Virgin River between thousand-foot canyon walls, no trail, just the riverbed.
places.tip: Rent water shoes and a walking stick in Springdale — regular hiking boots get miserable fast.

places.name: Angels Landing
places.description: A chain-assisted scramble up a narrow sandstone fin with 1,000-ft drop-offs on both sides, ending at one of the best views in Zion.
places.tip: Requires a permit lottery — apply in advance, don't show up hoping for a walk-up spot.

places.name: Highway 128 (Colorado River Scenic Byway)
places.description: Follows the Colorado River past towering red rock cliffs between Moab and I-70 — one of the most scenic river drives in the Southwest.
places.tip: Great for golden-hour light on the cliffs; pairs well with a stop in Moab.

places.name: Delicate Arch Trail
places.description: The 3-mile roundtrip hike to Utah's most iconic arch, exposed slickrock most of the way with a payoff view over Salt Valley.
places.tip: Go for sunset — the arch glows orange and it's the single most photographed moment in the state.

places.name: Moab off-road & mountain biking
places.description: White Rim Road, Slickrock Trail, and a genuine off-road/mountain-biking capital of the Southwest, for those who want more adrenaline than a hike offers.
places.tip: Rent or shuttle-tour if you don't have your own 4WD or full-suspension bike.

places.name: Zion National Park
places.description: Utah's most-visited park — towering sandstone cliffs, the Virgin River, and trails ranging from flat riverside walks to Angels Landing.
places.tip: The park uses a shuttle system in peak season; personal vehicles aren't allowed up-canyon then.

places.name: Bryce Canyon National Park
places.description: Thousands of orange hoodoo spires packed into a natural amphitheater — genuinely otherworldly, and one of the best stargazing spots in the country.
places.tip: The rim trail viewpoints are stunning even for non-hikers; sunrise light is the best time to see the hoodoos glow.

places.name: Arches National Park
places.description: Home to Delicate Arch and over 2,000 other natural stone arches in a compact, easy-to-explore park.
places.tip: Check the current year's entry rules before you go — the reservation system has changed multiple times.

places.name: Canyonlands National Park
places.description: Vast, rugged canyon country carved by the Colorado and Green Rivers — Island in the Sky is the most accessible of its three districts, with dramatic overlooks.
places.tip: Come for sunrise or sunset at Grand View Point — the light across the canyons is dramatic.

places.name: Capitol Reef National Park
places.description: The least crowded of the Mighty Five — a 100-mile 'waterpocket fold' of colorful cliffs, with historic orchards you can pick fruit from in season.
places.tip: Quieter than the other four parks — a good choice if you want the scenery without the crowds.

places.name: Temple Square, Salt Lake City
places.description: The historic heart of Salt Lake City and headquarters of the LDS Church, with gardens, museums, and architecture worth a half-day even for non-visitors of the faith.
places.tip: Free to visit and walk through; a good stop if you're flying in or out of Salt Lake.

places.name: Goblin Valley State Park
places.description: Thousands of small mushroom-shaped hoodoos — 'goblins' — spread across a valley you're free to wander and climb among, unlike the more restricted major parks.
places.tip: Far less crowded than the Mighty Five and genuinely fun to explore off-trail.

places.name: Valley of the Gods
places.description: A quieter, free alternative to Monument Valley with similar towering red rock monoliths and a scenic dirt loop road.
places.tip: The unpaved loop road is doable in a regular car in dry weather, but check conditions after rain.

places.name: Kanarraville Falls
places.description: A slot canyon hike that has you wading through Kanarra Creek repeatedly before reaching a waterfall inside the narrows.
places.tip: You will get wet — bring water shoes or old sneakers you don't mind soaking.

places.name: Cathedral Valley
places.description: Remote backcountry section of Capitol Reef with giant monolith formations and almost no visitors, thanks to the river crossing and dirt road required to reach it.
places.tip: Needs a high-clearance 4WD vehicle and a river ford at the start — not for a rental sedan.

places.name: Mystic Hot Springs
places.description: Mineral hot springs in converted clawfoot tubs (and even old buses you can stay in) in the small desert town of Monroe — a genuinely quirky, off-the-radar soak.
places.tip: Not much else around — come for the springs specifically, not as a day-trip base.

places.name: Sand Hollow State Park
places.description: Vivid orange-red sand dunes against a turquoise reservoir — a popular ATV and off-road spot that most Zion-bound travelers drive right past.
places.tip: Rent an ATV locally in St. George if you don't have your own.

places.name: Fry sauce
places.description: A ketchup-mayo blend invented at Arctic Circle, a Utah-born fast food chain — locals argue fiercely over the right ratio.

places.name: Funeral potatoes
places.description: A cheesy potato casserole traditionally served by LDS church Relief Societies after funerals — now a broader Utah comfort-food staple.

places.name: Utah scones
places.description: Not a British scone at all — deep-fried pioneer-era dough served hot with honey butter.

places.name: Dirty sodas
places.description: Soda mixed with cream and flavored syrups, popularized by Utah chain Swig — a ritual much like a coffee run elsewhere in the country.

places.name: Pioneer Day (July 24)
places.description: A state holiday commemorating the first Mormon pioneers reaching Salt Lake Valley in 1847 — paired unofficially with 'Pie and Beer Day' at local breweries.

places.name: Green chile at Red Iguana
places.description: A Salt Lake City institution for Utah's take on Mexican cuisine, especially its mole sauces.

name: Maine
hero_tagline: Granite cliffs dropping straight into the Atlantic, and a lobster roll at the end of every trail
hero_description: The only national park in the Northeast, a coastline built for lighthouse-hopping, and small harbor towns that feel a world away from the rest of the East Coast.
best_time_to_visit: June-August for the warmest weather and full services, but September-October is increasingly considered Maine's best season — cooler, quieter, and timed with peak fall foliage.
altitude_or_climate_note: Coastal weather changes fast — pack layers even in summer, since evenings on Mount Desert Island get cold regardless of the daytime temperature.
permits_note: Cadillac Mountain's summit road requires a separate timed-entry vehicle reservation for sunrise viewing in season — book this specifically, it's not covered by the general park pass.
gear_note: Good grip footwear for granite scrambling on trails like the Beehive and Precipice — these involve iron rungs and real exposure, not just a walk.

places.name: Precipice Trail
places.description: An adrenaline hike up iron rungs and narrow ledges bolted into a cliff face — one of the most exposed trails in any Eastern national park.
places.tip: Closed seasonally for peregrine falcon nesting — check status before you go.

places.name: Beehive Trail
places.description: A tamer cousin of the Precipice with cliff walks and metal rungs but less exposure — still a genuine adventure with a big payoff view.
places.tip: Popular — go early to avoid a queue at the rung sections.

places.name: Penobscot-Sargent Loop
places.description: A full-day traverse connecting two of Acadia's highest peaks, much of it above treeline on open granite ridgeline.
places.tip: Requires good fitness and some route-finding over open rock — not a casual stroll.

places.name: Park Loop Road
places.description: Acadia's signature scenic drive, passing Thunder Hole, Sand Beach, and Otter Cliff along the park's rocky coastline.
places.tip: Closed December through mid-April — a summer/fall drive only.

places.name: Cadillac Mountain sunrise
places.description: The highest point on the US Atlantic coast, and — for part of the year — the first place in the country to see the sunrise.
places.tip: Needs its own separate timed-entry vehicle reservation in season, booked ahead.

places.name: Schoodic Peninsula
places.description: A quieter, mainland section of Acadia about 45 minutes from Mount Desert Island, with the same granite-and-ocean scenery and a fraction of the crowds.
places.tip: A good half-day add-on if Bar Harbor itself feels too busy.

places.name: Bar Harbor
places.description: The gateway town to Acadia National Park and Mount Desert Island — restaurants, shops, and boat tours alongside some of the best coastal scenery in New England.
places.tip: Summer is peak season and genuinely crowded — the Island Explorer shuttle is worth using instead of driving.

places.name: Thunder Hole & Otter Cliff
places.description: A rock inlet where waves crash with a booming sound at the right tide, right along Ocean Path with Otter Cliff nearby.
places.tip: Time your visit around mid-to-rising tide for the loudest 'thunder.'

places.name: Portland Head Light
places.description: Maine's oldest and most photographed lighthouse, in Cape Elizabeth just outside Portland.
places.tip: The surrounding Fort Williams Park is free and a nice spot for a picnic with the lighthouse view.

places.name: Old Port, Portland
places.description: Portland's historic waterfront district — cobblestone streets, seafood restaurants, and a genuinely walkable small-city feel.
places.tip: The Downeaster train connects Portland to Boston if you don't want to drive.

places.name: Camden
places.description: A classic Maine harbor town with Mount Battie's short hike overlooking the bay and windjammer sailboats in the harbor.
places.tip: Combine with the Portland-to-Bar Harbor drive — it's directly on the route.

places.name: Ocean Path
places.description: A flat, easy 4.5-mile roundtrip coastal path connecting Sand Beach to Otter Point — the most accessible way to see Acadia's coastline on foot.
places.tip: Good for families or anyone wanting Acadia's views without the exposed cliff hikes.

places.name: Isle au Haut
places.description: A secluded island section of Acadia reachable only by mail boat — coastal hiking trails and a peaceful fishing village with almost none of the mainland's crowds.
places.tip: Plan around the mail boat schedule — this isn't a spontaneous same-day trip.

places.name: Schoodic Peninsula's Alder & Blueberry Hill trails
places.description: Quiet woodland and coastal trails on the mainland section of Acadia, with a fraction of Mount Desert Island's foot traffic.
places.tip: Go for solitude, not for the single biggest view — this is the anti-crowd version of Acadia.

places.name: Shackford Head State Park
places.description: Rugged coastal bluffs near Eastport — the easternmost city in the US — on a peninsula that was once slated for an oil refinery before becoming parkland instead.
places.tip: A genuine off-the-radar stop for travelers going all the way Downeast.

places.name: West Quoddy Head Lighthouse
places.description: The easternmost point in the continental US, marked by a distinctive red-and-white striped lighthouse — most visitors never make it this far Downeast.
places.tip: A long drive from Bar Harbor — best combined with Shackford Head and Eastport as a dedicated Downeast day.

places.name: Blue Hill
places.description: A low-key coastal town with few dedicated attractions but genuine small-town Maine charm, well off the Bar Harbor tourist circuit.
places.tip: Go for the atmosphere and quiet, not for a checklist of sights.

places.name: Great Wass Island
places.description: Remote Downeast coastal hiking through peat bogs and rocky shoreline, well beyond where most Acadia visitors ever travel.
places.tip: Bring your own supplies — services thin out considerably this far Downeast.

places.name: Lobster roll
places.description: Maine's signature dish — fresh lobster meat with mayo or drawn butter on a toasted split-top bun.

places.name: Whoopie pie
places.description: Two soft cake rounds with cream filling — Maine has embraced it as a cultural symbol (Pennsylvania also claims it).

places.name: Fried clams
places.description: Cold Maine waters produce especially tender clams, cornmeal-battered and fried, a seafood-shack staple.

places.name: Wild blueberries
places.description: Maine is the largest producer of wild (not cultivated) blueberries in the US — look for them in pies and at farm stands.

places.name: Maine Lobster Festival
places.description: Held annually in Rockland, one of the state's biggest food-culture events.

places.name: French-Canadian influence
places.description: Dishes like tourtière (a meat pie) reflect Maine's French-Canadian heritage, especially in northern Maine near the Quebec border.

name: California
hero_tagline: Redwood forests, red rock deserts, and a coastline that never stops changing
hero_description: The most geographically diverse state in the country — granite peaks in Yosemite, foggy redwood coastline, and Mediterranean wine country, all reachable inside a week.
best_time_to_visit: April-May and September-October for mild weather and thinner crowds statewide. Summer (June-August) is peak season and the busiest at Yosemite, Tahoe, and the beaches; late April-May is peak waterfall season in Yosemite specifically.
altitude_or_climate_note: California's regions run on completely different weather clocks at once — coastal fog, desert heat, and Sierra snow can all be happening the same week. Check conditions for your specific stops, not just "California" broadly.
permits_note: Half Dome (Yosemite) requires a separate permit lottery. Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road close in winter and typically don't reopen until May or June.
gear_note: Layers regardless of season — coastal fog burns off by afternoon but mornings run cold, and Sierra elevations are cold year-round after dark.

places.name: Mist Trail to Vernal & Nevada Falls
places.description: Yosemite's most popular hike for good reason — a granite staircase alongside the Merced River that mists you as you climb, with two waterfalls as the payoff.
places.tip: Starts crowded; go early morning to beat both the heat and the tour groups.

places.name: Tioga Road
places.description: Crosses Yosemite at nearly 10,000 ft through Tuolumne Meadows, with far fewer crowds than the Valley floor below.
places.tip: Closed roughly November-May depending on snowpack — check status before planning around it.

places.name: Highway 1 through Big Sur
places.description: A 90-mile stretch of the Pacific Coast Highway between Carmel and San Simeon — redwood-lined canyons dropping straight to the ocean.
places.tip: Give it a full day; the pullouts and short hikes are the point, not the drive time.

places.name: Kings Canyon Scenic Byway
places.description: One of the most underrated drives in the state — sequoia groves, granite cliffs, and a canyon deeper than the Grand Canyon in places, with a fraction of Yosemite's traffic.
places.tip: Stop at General Grant Grove and, if you have energy left, the Mist Falls Trail.

places.name: Half Dome
places.description: Yosemite's ultimate day hike — a cable-assisted final ascent up a sheer granite dome, for those who plan far enough ahead to get a permit.
places.tip: Permit lottery required; apply months in advance.

places.name: Bobcat Trail, Andrew Molera State Park
places.description: An easy 6-mile roundtrip through redwood forest along the Big Sur River — a gentler way to experience Big Sur's ecosystem beyond the highway pullouts.
places.tip: Combine with a stop at Point Lobos State Reserve nearby.

places.name: Yosemite National Park
places.description: California's signature national park — Half Dome, El Capitan, and waterfalls that draw climbers and hikers from around the world.
places.tip: The Valley floor gets very congested in summer; consider Tioga Road or Wawona for a quieter angle.

places.name: Golden Gate Bridge & San Francisco
places.description: The iconic bridge plus a genuinely walkable city — Alcatraz, cable cars, and some of the best food in the country.
places.tip: Best visited September-November when the famous SF fog lifts most consistently.

places.name: Hollywood & Santa Monica, Los Angeles
places.description: The Hollywood Sign, Santa Monica Pier, and beach culture — LA's classic first-timer circuit.
places.tip: LA is deeply car-dependent; budget real time for traffic between neighborhoods.

places.name: Napa & Sonoma Valley
places.description: California's wine country — vineyard tours and tastings against rolling gold-and-green hills.
places.tip: Harvest season (September-October) is the most atmospheric, if also the busiest.

places.name: Lake Tahoe
places.description: A high-Sierra lake that's a summer boating and hiking destination and a winter ski destination in the same place.
places.tip: Pick your season deliberately — the vibe and activities completely flip between summer and winter.

places.name: Lost Coast
places.description: California's most remote stretch of coastline — no highway runs along it, so it stays wild, quiet, and largely undeveloped.
places.tip: Backpacking the full Lost Coast Trail takes real planning; a shorter out-and-back is fine for a day visit.

places.name: Black Sand Beach, Marin Headlands
places.description: A black-sand beach just north of San Francisco in Sausalito — most visitors never realize it's this close to the city.
places.tip: Easy add-on to a Marin Headlands day trip; pair with the Golden Gate overlook.

places.name: Lassen Volcanic National Park
places.description: Yosemite's much smaller, far less crowded sibling — active volcanic features, alpine lakes, and similar granite-and-forest scenery without the traffic.
places.tip: A genuine alternative if Yosemite's crowds are the dealbreaker.

places.name: Tuolumne Meadows
places.description: Yosemite's high country along Tioga Road — a grassy alpine plain with a fraction of the Valley's foot traffic.
places.tip: Good base for the Cathedral Lakes or Elizabeth Lake hikes if you want solitude.

places.name: Ojai Valley
places.description: A Mediterranean-climate valley near Ventura County known for its 'Pink Moment' sunsets, natural hot springs, and Los Padres National Forest hiking.
places.tip: A relaxed, artsy alternative to the busier Central Coast towns.

places.name: Alabama Hills
places.description: Boulder-strewn high desert near Lone Pine that's stood in for hundreds of Western films — dramatic rock formations with Mt. Whitney as a backdrop.
places.tip: Mobius Arch at sunrise or sunset is the classic shot.

places.name: In-N-Out Burger
places.description: Born from 1960s LA surfer culture — a fast-food chain now inseparable from California identity.

places.name: Fish tacos
places.description: A Baja California import via Southern California's border-adjacent food culture.

places.name: Napa & Sonoma wine culture
places.description: World-class wine country with harvest-season festivals like the Napa Valley Wine & Food Festival.

places.name: Farm-to-table (NorCal) vs. fusion (SoCal)
places.description: Northern California leans into seasonal, locally-sourced dining; Southern California is a melting pot of Mexican, Korean, Vietnamese, and Mediterranean fusion.

places.name: Sourdough bread
places.description: A San Francisco staple made with a natural yeast starter, traditionally paired with clam chowder.

places.name: Monterey Jazz and Food Festival
places.description: Pairs the state's food culture with live jazz — one of many California food-and-music festivals.

name: Wyoming
hero_tagline: Geysers, grizzlies, and the jagged skyline of the Tetons
hero_description: Home to the world's first national park and its dramatic mountain neighbor — geothermal wonders, some of the best wildlife-watching in the Lower 48, and a road connecting the two that's a destination in itself.
best_time_to_visit: Mid-June through early October, when roads, trails, and visitor services are fully open across both parks. Late June-early July brings peak wildflowers; September brings elk rut and thinner crowds.
altitude_or_climate_note: This is active grizzly bear habitat — carry bear spray on any hike, know how to use it, and avoid hiking alone in backcountry areas. Weather turns fast at altitude even in summer.
permits_note: Backcountry camping in Yellowstone or Grand Teton requires a permit. No timed-entry system for the parks themselves, but Jenny Lake parking fills very early in peak season.
gear_note: Bear spray (rentable near Canyon Village in Yellowstone), layers for sudden weather shifts, and a printed map — cell service is minimal to nonexistent through most of both parks.

places.name: Beartooth Highway
places.description: One of the highest paved roads in the US, connecting Yellowstone's northeast entrance to Red Lodge, Montana, with switchbacks above 10,000 ft.
places.tip: Open roughly Memorial Day-mid October only; check for closures after early or late-season snow.

places.name: Paintbrush Canyon–Cascade Canyon Loop
places.description: Grand Teton's best full-day hike, passing Jenny Lake, Inspiration Point, Lake Solitude, and sweeping views of the Teton range in one route.
places.tip: A serious full-day undertaking — start early and check trail conditions for snow at the higher pass.

places.name: Grand Prismatic via Fairy Falls Trail
places.description: An easy 0.6-mile hike to an overlook above Yellowstone's largest hot spring — the only way to actually see its full rainbow color, which is invisible from the boardwalk below.
places.tip: The boardwalk view alone doesn't show the colors — the overlook is worth the short extra hike.

places.name: Jenny Lake to Hidden Falls & Inspiration Point
places.description: Take the shuttle boat across Jenny Lake, then hike up to a waterfall and a canyon-mouth viewpoint over Jackson Hole.
places.tip: Arrive 30 minutes before the boat shuttle opens — the parking lot fills fast.

places.name: Mount Washburn
places.description: A strenuous 6-mile roundtrip to a 10,243-ft summit with 360-degree views and good odds of spotting bighorn sheep.
places.tip: Exposed above treeline for the final stretch — watch for afternoon thunderstorms.

places.name: String Lake Loop
places.description: An easy, flat 3-mile loop around the shallowest, warmest lake in the Tetons — genuinely swimmable, unlike most alpine lakes here.
places.tip: A good lower-effort option paired with the Jenny Lake shuttle day.

places.name: Old Faithful & Upper Geyser Basin
places.description: Yellowstone's most famous geyser, erupting roughly every 90 minutes, surrounded by the highest concentration of geysers on Earth.
places.tip: Check the predicted eruption time at the visitor center rather than waiting blind.

places.name: Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
places.description: A dramatically colored canyon carved by the Yellowstone River, with two major waterfalls and multiple viewpoints along both rims.
places.tip: Artist Point on the South Rim is the classic view.

places.name: Jackson Hole
places.description: The classic gateway town to Grand Teton — western storefronts, a lively food scene, and easy access into the park.
places.tip: Book lodging well ahead in summer; it's the main base for both parks.

places.name: Jenny Lake
places.description: Grand Teton's most photographed lake, framed directly by the mountain range, with boat shuttles and trailheads right at the shore.
places.tip: The most crowded single spot in the park — arrive early or expect a wait.

places.name: Lamar Valley
places.description: Called the 'Serengeti of North America' for its wildlife density — bison, wolves, and bears are regularly spotted from the road.
places.tip: Dawn and dusk are by far the best times for wildlife activity.

places.name: Black Sand Basin
places.description: A small, colorful geyser basin just northwest of Old Faithful with the Cliff Geyser and Rainbow Pool — a fraction of the crowds of the main basin next door.
places.tip: Walkable from the Upper Geyser Basin trail network — no separate long drive needed.

places.name: Trout Lake, Lamar Valley
places.description: A short, steep 1.2-mile roundtrip to a crystal-clear lake, best combined with a dawn wildlife-watching drive through Lamar Valley.
places.tip: Go at first light for both the wildlife and the quietest trail experience.

places.name: Bunsen Peak Loop
places.description: A 4.6-mile hike with panoramic views over Mammoth Hot Springs and the Yellowstone River, hiked as a loop via the old road for a better experience than the direct route.
places.tip: Growing in popularity but still far quieter than Mount Washburn.

places.name: Sedge Bay
places.description: A quiet pebble beach on Yellowstone Lake, good for a picnic and regular sightings of bison, elk, and bald eagles.
places.tip: A relaxed stop most visitors drive straight past.

places.name: Bechler Region
places.description: A remote southwest corner of Yellowstone known for waterfalls and backcountry hot springs, with a fraction of the park's total visitation.
places.tip: Facilities are minimal — come prepared for a more rustic, self-sufficient experience.

places.name: Firehole River Swimming Area
places.description: A geothermally warmed swimming spot in the Firehole River — one of the few places in the park where swimming is actually encouraged.
places.tip: A short detour off the main loop road near Firehole Spring — easy to miss if you don't know to look.

places.name: Bison steak & burgers
places.description: Grilled over open flame — a direct link to the animal's cultural significance in the state's ranching heritage.

places.name: Chuckwagon cooking
places.description: Traditional cowboy campfire cooking — steaks, beans, cornbread — still served at ranch cookouts across the state.

places.name: Cheyenne Frontier Days
places.description: The world's largest outdoor rodeo, running annually since 1897 — ten days in late July with a long-standing pancake breakfast tradition.

places.name: Rocky Mountain oysters
places.description: Shared with Colorado — a rodeo-circuit staple across cattle country.

places.name: Cowboy culture
places.description: Wyoming's identity as 'the Cowboy State' shows up in ranching traditions, rodeo, and Western art found in towns like Cheyenne.

name: Arizona
hero_tagline: The Grand Canyon is just the headline act
hero_description: Red rock, slot canyons, and one of the seven natural wonders of the world — plus a surprising amount of pine forest and cool mountain towns once you get away from the desert floor.
best_time_to_visit: Spring (March-May) and fall (September-November) — warm days without the brutal summer heat. Summer temperatures regularly exceed 100°F at lower elevations like Phoenix and the Grand Canyon's inner canyon.
altitude_or_climate_note: Heat is the real hazard here, not cold — hiking below the Grand Canyon's rim in summer has caused real medical emergencies. Carry far more water than feels necessary and avoid midday exertion at lower elevations.
permits_note: The Grand Canyon's North Rim is only open roughly mid-May through mid-October due to snow. Permits are required for overnight backcountry camping below the rim.
gear_note: A high-clearance vehicle helps around Sedona's backcountry trailheads (not required for the main sites). Sun protection matters more than warmth most of the year.

places.name: South Kaibab or Bright Angel Trail (below the rim)
places.description: Hiking below the Grand Canyon's rim shows a completely different side of the canyon than any viewpoint can — but these trails should only be attempted with serious water and heat preparation.
places.tip: Do not attempt a rim-to-river-and-back hike in one day in summer — heat-related rescues are common.

places.name: Oak Creek Canyon Drive (Highway 89A)
places.description: A 22-mile drive climbing 2,500 feet from Sedona to Flagstaff through towering canyon walls and pine forest — rated one of the most scenic drives in America.
places.tip: Combine with a stop at Slide Rock State Park's natural swimming hole partway up.

places.name: Boynton Canyon Trail
places.description: A red-rock hike past Ancestral Puebloan ruins and a hidden cave formation called the Subway, ending near the Kachina Woman spire.
places.tip: One of Sedona's more spiritually significant sites — go early to avoid both heat and crowds.

places.name: Red Rock Scenic Byway (Highway 179)
places.description: The direct route into Sedona past Bell Rock and Cathedral Rock, with pullouts for photos at nearly every turn.
places.tip: Bell Rock and Courthouse Butte have an easy loop trail if you want to get out of the car.

places.name: Sedona to Grand Canyon via Sunset Crater & Wupatki
places.description: The scenic alternative to the direct highway — passes an ancient volcano and Ancestral Puebloan ruins on the way to the canyon's East Entrance.
places.tip: Adds a couple of hours but is far more interesting than the direct route.

places.name: Camelback Mountain
places.description: Phoenix's signature hike — a steep scramble with sweeping views over the whole Valley, best done before sunrise heat sets in.
places.tip: Pair with nearby Piestewa Peak or Papago Park if you want a second, easier hike the same trip.

places.name: Grand Canyon South Rim
places.description: The classic Grand Canyon visit — accessible viewpoints, the historic village, and sunrise or sunset from any of the rim overlooks.
places.tip: The South Rim is open year-round, unlike the North Rim.

places.name: Sedona
places.description: Red rock formations, a genuinely vibrant arts scene, and some of the most photographed scenery in the Southwest.
places.tip: A free shuttle runs to popular trailheads in peak season — worth using instead of hunting for parking.

places.name: Horseshoe Bend
places.description: A dramatic overlook of the Colorado River curling almost 270 degrees around a sandstone bluff, near Page.
places.tip: The walk to the viewpoint is short but exposed and can be brutally hot midday in summer.

places.name: Antelope Canyon
places.description: A famously photogenic slot canyon with light beams and sculpted sandstone walls — visitable only with a guided tour.
places.tip: Book the tour well in advance; access is controlled entirely by Navajo Nation guides.

places.name: Grand Canyon North Rim
places.description: A higher-elevation, more secluded alternative to the South Rim, with a genuinely different feel and far fewer visitors.
places.tip: Only open roughly mid-May through mid-October — check dates before planning around it.

places.name: Tonto Natural Bridge State Park
places.description: Hidden in the pine forests near Payson — believed to be the world's largest natural travertine bridge, 183 feet high, tucked into central Arizona's mountains.
places.tip: A genuinely surprising stop for anyone who thinks Arizona is all desert.

places.name: Fay Canyon Trail
places.description: An easy, largely overlooked Sedona hike leading to a natural arch and a quiet viewpoint most visitors skip in favor of Bell Rock.
places.tip: A good choice when the more famous Sedona trailheads are packed.

places.name: Sycamore Canyon
places.description: Arizona's second-largest gorge after the Grand Canyon itself, with a scenic loop drive and far fewer visitors than either Sedona or the canyon.
places.tip: Stop at Sycamore Canyon Vista for the classic overlook shot.

places.name: Bill Williams Mountain
places.description: A quiet forested peak near Williams reachable by trail or, with a high-clearance vehicle, a dirt road most visitors never realize exists.
places.tip: A good stop on the Sedona-to-Grand Canyon drive that almost nobody takes.

places.name: Slide Rock State Park
places.description: A natural sandstone waterslide and swimming hole in Oak Creek Canyon — a genuine cool-off spot most Grand Canyon-bound travelers drive right past.
places.tip: Visit November-February for the cheapest, least crowded experience per local advice, or midday in summer to actually use the water.

places.name: Mescal Trailhead to Mescal Mountain
places.description: An intermediate Sedona hike to a large sandstone butte with views into Boynton Canyon — well off the main tourist circuit.
places.tip: Quieter than the Bell Rock and Cathedral Rock trails nearby.

places.name: Sonoran Mexican cuisine
places.description: Distinct from Tex-Mex or California-Mexican — carne asada, mesquite-fired grills, and cowboy beans rooted in the Sonoran Desert that spans the AZ-Mexico border.

places.name: Navajo tacos
places.description: Fry bread topped with beans, red chili, and cheese — a Native American dish found at Native-owned eateries statewide.

places.name: Sonoran hot dog
places.description: A bacon-wrapped hot dog loaded with toppings, born in Hermosillo, Sonora and now an Arizona late-night staple.

places.name: Cheese crisp
places.description: Arizona's 'unofficial appetizer' — an open-faced crisped tortilla with melted cheese, rooted in Sonoran ranch cooking.

places.name: Tucson, UNESCO City of Gastronomy
places.description: The first American city to receive this designation, recognizing its Native American, Mexican, and Spanish colonial culinary layers.

places.name: Desert-foraged ingredients
places.description: Prickly pear, cholla buds, tepary beans, and chiltepin chiles — ingredients Indigenous peoples (Tohono O'odham, Navajo, Hopi, Apache) have used for thousands of years.

name: Tennessee
hero_tagline: The most-visited national park in America, and it's not close
hero_description: Great Smoky Mountains National Park draws more visitors than Yellowstone and Grand Canyon combined — mist-covered ridgelines, historic mountain settlements, and hiking for every ability level, with music-city energy waiting in Nashville if you want a change of pace.
best_time_to_visit: Spring (April-May) for wildflowers and waterfalls at peak flow with thinner crowds, or fall (October) for foliage — though fall is also the single busiest month, so book ahead. Summer is popular but hot and humid.
altitude_or_climate_note: Cell service is spotty throughout the park — download offline maps before you go. Spring hiking can be wet; afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer.
permits_note: No park entrance fee, but a parking tag ($5/day or annual options) is required for any vehicle parked more than 15 minutes. Kuwohi Road closes December-March; Roaring Fork Motor Trail closes in late November.
gear_note: Sturdy footwear for creek crossings on several trails, layers for the elevation swing between Gatlinburg and the high ridgelines, and a paper map as backup for the dead zones.

places.name: Alum Cave Trail to Mount LeConte
places.description: One of the most popular strenuous hikes in the park — a cave-like bluff formation partway up, and one of the best-maintained routes to a genuine mountain summit.
places.tip: Start early; parking at the trailhead fills up fast on weekends.

places.name: Newfound Gap Road (US-441)
places.description: The most complete scenic drive in the Smokies, crossing the entire park from Gatlinburg to Cherokee and climbing from 1,300 to over 5,000 ft, with the forest visibly changing as you climb.
places.tip: Open year-round, unlike several other park roads — a reliable option even in shoulder season.

places.name: Cades Cove Loop
places.description: An 11-mile loop past historic homesteads, churches, and some of the best wildlife-spotting odds in the park — genuinely worth a half day on its own.
places.tip: Go at dawn for both wildlife activity and to beat the traffic this loop is famous for.

places.name: Kuwohi (Clingmans Dome) Observation Tower
places.description: At 6,643 ft, the highest point in the park, with a spiral observation tower and a lesser-known tunnel underneath.
places.tip: Road closes December-March — check seasonal status before planning around it.

places.name: Rainbow Falls Trail
places.description: A moderately strenuous hike to one of the tallest single-drop waterfalls in the park, best after spring rains when flow is highest.
places.tip: Can be crowded near the falls itself — the payoff view is worth the wait.

places.name: Foothills Parkway
places.description: Ridge-top views along the park's northern edge that rival the more famous Blue Ridge Parkway, with a fraction of the traffic.
places.tip: A good alternative when Newfound Gap Road feels too busy.

places.name: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
places.description: America's most-visited national park — accessible trails, historic structures, and mountain scenery straddling Tennessee and North Carolina.
places.tip: No entrance fee, but a parking tag is required for stops over 15 minutes.

places.name: Gatlinburg
places.description: The main gateway town to the park — restaurants, shops, and easy access, if a bit touristy at its core.
places.tip: Stay here for convenience, but expect crowds in peak season.

places.name: Laurel Falls Trail
places.description: A paved, family-friendly trail to an 80-ft waterfall — one of the most accessible hikes with a real payoff in the whole park.
places.tip: Popular with families; go early for a quieter experience.

places.name: Nashville
places.description: Country music's capital — live honky-tonks on Broadway, the Grand Ole Opry, and a food scene that's grown well beyond its music-city reputation.
places.tip: A different pace entirely from the mountains — good as a bookend to a Smokies trip rather than a day trip from it.

places.name: Abrams Falls Trail
places.description: A moderate 5-mile roundtrip off the Cades Cove Loop to a powerful, wide waterfall.
places.tip: Combine with the Cades Cove Loop drive for one efficient day.

places.name: Cosby section waterfall hike
places.description: A 4-mile roundtrip in the least-visited of the park's three main entrances, ending at a 90-ft waterfall that fans across a wide rock face — often empty on summer weekdays.
places.tip: Also one of the best spots in the park for synchronous firefly activity in late May-mid June.

places.name: Elkmont Ghost Town
places.description: A collection of abandoned early-1900s vacation cottages reached via a quiet forest nature trail — an eerie, little-visited piece of the park's history.
places.tip: A short, easy add-on if you're already near the Elkmont campground area.

places.name: Rhododendron Creek Trail
places.description: A quiet loop hike past small waterfalls and an old cemetery, with the remains of a steam engine visible in the creek bed — genuinely uncrowded even in peak season.
places.tip: Lacks big sweeping views, but makes up for it in solitude.

places.name: Upper Tremont Road
places.description: A quieter scenic drive along the Middle Prong of the Little River, well off the main Newfound Gap/Cades Cove circuit.
places.tip: A good choice for a slow afternoon with fewer cars around.

places.name: Middle Prong Thunderhead Prong Trail
places.description: A short, gentle, secluded hike following a river tributary to a boulder-strewn cascade — an easy escape from the park's busier corridors.
places.tip: Good option for families wanting a quiet short walk rather than a summit push.

places.name: Nashville hot chicken
places.description: Fried chicken coated in a fiery spice paste, said to originate from Prince's Hot Chicken Shack — as core to Nashville's identity as country music.

places.name: Memphis dry-rub BBQ
places.description: Ribs and pulled pork smoked over hickory, dry-rubbed rather than sauced — The Rendezvous is the classic spot.

places.name: Beale Street blues
places.description: Memphis's historic music strip — live blues, soul, and rockabilly alongside the city's barbecue scene.

places.name: Country Music Hall of Fame & Grand Ole Opry
places.description: Nashville's status as the Country Music Capital of the World, with live shows and museum culture built around it.

places.name: Banana pudding
places.description: A Southern classic dessert found on menus statewide, alongside biscuits and gravy and sweet tea.

places.name: African American culinary heritage
places.description: Hot chicken and much of Tennessee's barbecue tradition trace directly to African American culinary contributions.

name: Louisiana
hero_tagline: Cypress swamps by day, brass bands by night
hero_description: French, Spanish, African, Caribbean, and Acadian influences layered over three centuries — the result is a state where the food and music are as much the destination as the scenery.
best_time_to_visit: March-May for the mildest weather and festival season (French Quarter Festival, Jazz Fest late April-early May). Avoid June-November if possible — hurricane season, with peak risk in August-September and brutal heat and humidity throughout.
altitude_or_climate_note: Flat, humid, and hurricane-exposed — check storm forecasts before any summer or fall trip, and consider travel insurance during hurricane season (June 1-November 30).
permits_note: No general park permits needed for swamp tours (book commercial operators directly). Mardi Gras parade viewing is free but book lodging months ahead for both Mardi Gras and Jazz Fest — rentals sell out early.
gear_note: Insect repellent and light, breathable clothing year-round in the swamps; water shoes for kayak-based swamp tours. Layers for spring/fall, when weather shifts fast.

places.name: Atchafalaya Basin kayaking
places.description: The largest swamp in the United States — paddle through cypress-tupelo wetlands teeming with alligators, herons, and one of the most biologically diverse environments in the country.
places.tip: Guided tours are worth it for the ecology and folklore context, not just navigation.

places.name: Tunica Hills Wildlife Management Area
places.description: A genuine surprise in famously flat Louisiana — rugged trails through rolling hills and bluffs, with hidden waterfalls and wildflower meadows.
places.tip: The rare hilly terrain makes this stand out from the rest of the state's hiking.

places.name: Honey Island Swamp kayak tour
places.description: A quieter, more secluded swamp tour option than the busier Atchafalaya routes, with a strong reputation among paddlers for solitude.
places.tip: Good pick if the more commercial swamp tours feel too crowded.

places.name: Avery Island
places.description: Home to the Tabasco factory and Jungle Gardens — tranquil lagoons, towering live oaks, and an unexpected ancient Buddha statue in the botanical gardens.
places.tip: Combine the factory tour with a walk through the gardens for a full half-day.

places.name: Kisatchie Hills
places.description: Louisiana's only National Forest, with genuinely hilly terrain for camping and hiking most visitors don't associate with the state.
places.tip: Pair with kayaking on nearby Toledo Bend Lake for a full outdoor day.

places.name: Grand Isle
places.description: Louisiana's only inhabited barrier island — fishing, birding, and a genuine beach vacation feel most visitors don't expect from the state.
places.tip: Best April-June and September-October.

places.name: French Quarter
places.description: New Orleans' oldest neighborhood — Jackson Square, St. Louis Cathedral, Café du Monde, and the architecture that defines the city's image worldwide.
places.tip: Go early morning for the same streets without the crowds or nighttime chaos.

places.name: Bourbon Street
places.description: The city's most famous nightlife strip — live brass bands, historic bars, and the birthplace of the Hurricane cocktail at Pat O'Brien's.
places.tip: Best experienced a few hours before and after sunset, before or after the rowdiest late-night crowds.

places.name: Plantation homes (Oak Alley & Whitney)
places.description: Oak Alley's iconic oak-lined path and Whitney Plantation's memorial to enslaved people offer two very different, both essential, sides of the region's history.
places.tip: Visiting both back to back gives a fuller, more honest picture than either alone.

places.name: Lafayette
places.description: The heart of Cajun Country and often called the 'Happiest City in America' — deep-rooted food, music, and Cajun traditions away from the New Orleans crowds.
places.tip: A good base for exploring Cajun Country's swamp tours and small towns.

places.name: Vermilionville
places.description: A living history village in Lafayette bringing 18th- and 19th-century Acadian culture to life with restored homes, crafts, and folk music.
places.tip: Especially vivid during spring and fall festival season.

places.name: Bluebonnet Swamp Nature Center
places.description: An easy, family-friendly boardwalk through cypress-tupelo swamp just outside Baton Rouge — a real wilderness feel minutes from the state capital.
places.tip: Morning visits with fog over the water are especially atmospheric.

places.name: Manchac Swamp kayak tour
places.description: A guided paddle through one of the state's most atmospheric, moss-draped swamps, quieter than the well-known New Orleans-adjacent tours.
places.tip: Go with a local guide who can point out wildlife you'd otherwise miss.

places.name: Bayou Des Cannes Trail
places.description: A moderate hike through cypress groves and bayous with real odds of spotting otters, herons, and even black bears.
places.tip: A genuine off-the-tourist-trail nature experience.

places.name: Natchitoches
places.description: Louisiana's oldest permanent settlement, with a well-preserved historic district and the state's famous Christmas Festival in December.
places.tip: A quieter, historic counterpoint to New Orleans if you want small-town Louisiana.

places.name: Courir de Mardi Gras (Cajun Country)
places.description: The rural, participatory version of Mardi Gras — horseback processions through the countryside, a world away from New Orleans parades.
places.tip: Happens around Mardi Gras season specifically in Cajun Country towns near Lafayette — plan ahead.

places.name: Gumbo, jambalaya & crawfish étouffée
places.description: The backbone of Cajun cooking, all built on the 'Holy Trinity' of onion, bell pepper, and celery — Louisiana's answer to French mirepoix.

places.name: Beignets & po'boys
places.description: Creole New Orleans' signature street food — powdered-sugar-dusted fried dough at Café du Monde, and overstuffed sandwiches piled with fried seafood or roast beef.

places.name: Cajun vs. Creole
places.description: Two distinct traditions, not one: Cajun is the rustic country cooking of Acadiana (descended from Acadian/Nova Scotian settlers); Creole is New Orleans' more refined French-and-Spanish-polished city cuisine.

places.name: New Orleans jazz
places.description: The birthplace of jazz — Preservation Hall for intimate traditional shows, Frenchmen Street for evolving live-music clubs.

places.name: Mardi Gras
places.description: A statewide celebration, not just a New Orleans parade — Cajun Country's Courir de Mardi Gras, zydeco music, and fais-do-dos offer a completely different, more participatory version.

places.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
places.description: Held the last weekend of April into the first weekend of May — daily performances spanning jazz, rock, gospel, hip-hop, and more.

name: Washington
hero_tagline: Three national parks, one loop, and a coffee culture that started it all
hero_description: Glacier-capped volcanoes, temperate rainforest, and 73 miles of wild Pacific coastline — all within a day's drive of a city that gave the world Starbucks and a genuinely serious independent coffee scene.
best_time_to_visit: July-September for the driest, warmest weather and full access to mountain passes and trails. Late July-August brings peak wildflowers at Mount Rainier's Paradise area. October is a local secret for Mount Baker's larch season with thinner crowds.
altitude_or_climate_note: The state's famous rain is concentrated on the western/coastal side — the Olympic Peninsula's rainforest gets over 12 feet of rain a year. Eastern Washington across the Cascades is dry and sunny by contrast.
permits_note: North Cascades' Colonial Creek Campground road closes November-May. Mount Rainier's roads to Paradise stay open year-round (chains required November-May) but most trails need summer conditions. Hurricane Ridge Road in Olympic closes in winter.
gear_note: A proper waterproof rain shell, not just water-resistant, if visiting the Olympic rainforest. Layers regardless of season — mountain weather changes fast even in summer.

places.name: Skyline Trail loop, Mount Rainier
places.description: The single best one-day hike in the park, climbing to Panorama Point at 6,800 ft with direct views of the Nisqually Glacier and, in July-August, wildflower meadows in full bloom.
places.tip: Starts from Paradise — arrive early, this is the park's most popular trailhead.

places.name: Hoh Rainforest
places.description: A genuinely otherworldly temperate rainforest hike in Olympic National Park — moss-draped maples and some of the wettest forest in the continental US.
places.tip: Combine with camping at Kalaloch or a hike out to Second Beach in La Push.

places.name: Sol Duc Falls & Hot Springs
places.description: A short hike to a scenic waterfall through narrow gorges, followed by a soak at the adjacent hot springs resort.
places.tip: A relaxing way to close out an Olympic Peninsula day of hiking.

places.name: Chain Lakes Loop, Mount Baker
places.description: A 7-mile circuit passing five lakes and crossing Ptarmigan Ridge with views of both Mount Baker and Mount Shuksan, staying above treeline most of the way.
places.tip: One of the rare trails where the payoff matches the effort at nearly every point.

places.name: Washington Pass & Cascade Loop
places.description: Liberty Bell's granite spires from the Washington Pass viewpoint, on the scenic drive into North Cascades — the least-visited of the state's three national parks.
places.tip: Pair with the Maple Pass hike just east of the park for a full day.

places.name: Wonderland Trail
places.description: A serious 93-mile loop circling all of Mount Rainier, with roughly 22,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain — a bucket-list multi-day trek for experienced hikers.
places.tip: Most hikers take 10-14 days; permits are competitive.

places.name: Pike Place Market
places.description: One of the oldest continuously operated public markets in the US, famous for its fish-throwing fishmongers and dating to 1907.
places.tip: Go early morning to see vendors setting up before the tour-bus crowds arrive.

places.name: Space Needle
places.description: Seattle's defining landmark, especially striking at night, with observation decks over Puget Sound and the skyline.
places.tip: Buy timed tickets in advance to skip the line.

places.name: Mount Rainier National Park
places.description: The highest peak in Washington at 14,411 ft and the most glaciated peak in the contiguous US, with Paradise as its most popular and accessible area.
places.tip: NPS reports visitation is up 40% over the last decade — expect real crowds at Paradise in summer.

places.name: Olympic National Park
places.description: A single park containing coastal beaches, alpine ridges, and temperate rainforest — genuinely three different ecosystems in one place.
places.tip: The park is vast; pick one or two areas rather than trying to see it all in a day.

places.name: Seattle coffee culture
places.description: The birthplace of Starbucks, but the real draw is the independent roaster scene, especially around Capitol Hill.
places.tip: Skip the original Starbucks tourist line and try a local independent roaster instead.

places.name: Heart O' the Forest Trail
places.description: An easy 4-mile roundtrip through pristine old-growth forest — the closest old-growth hike to Olympic's visitor center, with a fraction of the Hoh Rainforest's crowds.
places.tip: A good option when short on time but still wanting genuine old-growth forest.

places.name: Quinault Rain Forest
places.description: A pristine, far less-visited temperate rainforest in Olympic's southwest corner, with the Maple Glade loop and Kestner Homestead self-guided trail.
places.tip: About an hour from Forks — a quieter alternative to the more famous Hoh Rainforest.

places.name: North Cascades National Park
places.description: Washington's least-visited major park, thanks to challenging access roads and demanding terrain — jagged peaks and turquoise glacier lakes with real solitude.
places.tip: Fewer facilities than Rainier or Olympic — come prepared for a more rugged visit.

places.name: Ross Lake
places.description: A turquoise glacier-fed lake in North Cascades, reachable by trail or boat, with a fraction of the foot traffic of the state's more famous lakes.
places.tip: A good add-on to the Washington Pass scenic drive.

places.name: ʔálʔal Café, Pioneer Square
places.description: A Native-owned café inside the Chief Seattle Club serving Indigenous dishes like bison tacos and blue corn mush, alongside Native American art from Lummi and S'Klallam artists.
places.tip: As much a cultural stop as a meal — check current hours before visiting.

places.name: Cedar plank salmon
places.description: Fresh Pacific salmon cooked on a cedar plank, a method drawn directly from Pacific Northwest Native American cooking traditions.

places.name: Dungeness crab & geoduck
places.description: Fresh-caught Puget Sound shellfish — Dungeness crab is the local favorite, geoduck (a giant clam) is the adventurous try.

places.name: Independent coffee roasters
places.description: Seattle's coffee identity goes well beyond Starbucks — Capitol Hill in particular is dense with serious independent roasters.

places.name: Native American salmon traditions
places.description: Salmon is ceremonially significant to Pacific Northwest tribes, prepared in special ceremonies each year to honor the fish — still shaping how it's cooked and served today.

places.name: Marionberry pie
places.description: A Pacific Northwest blackberry cultivar, showing up in pies and desserts across the state as a genuinely regional specialty.

name: New Mexico
hero_tagline: The Land of Enchantment answers to one question first: red or green?
hero_description: Gypsum dunes, underground cave systems, ancient Pueblo cliff dwellings, and a food culture so distinct it has its own official state question — New Mexico rewards those willing to drive long distances between very different worlds.
best_time_to_visit: Spring (April-May) and fall (September-October) for mild temperatures. Late summer-early fall is chile harvest season, worth timing a trip around if food is a priority — the Hatch Chile Festival runs Labor Day weekend.
altitude_or_climate_note: New Mexico is genuinely remote in stretches — distances between sights are longer than they look on a map, and services thin out fast outside Albuquerque, Santa Fe, and Taos. High desert means big day-to-night temperature swings year-round.
permits_note: Carlsbad Caverns' Big Room self-guided tour takes about 1.5 hours; ranger-led tours require separate tickets and should be booked ahead. BLM land camping is widely available near Carlsbad and in remote areas — check current road conditions before driving out.
gear_note: Layers for the day-to-night temperature swing at altitude. Good closed shoes for both the caverns (cool, damp) and White Sands (hot, abrasive gypsum sand) — very different environments in the same state.

places.name: White Sands National Park
places.description: The largest gypsum dunefield in the world — pure white dunes you can sled down, hike into, or simply wander for a genuinely otherworldly landscape.
places.tip: Buy or rent a plastic sled at the visitor center; hike a bit further out for untrampled dunes.

places.name: Carlsbad Caverns
places.description: One of the most impressive cave systems in North America — descend into massive underground chambers via the Natural Entrance Trail or an elevator.
places.tip: Plan 3-4 hours; the Big Room self-guided loop alone takes about 1.5 hours.

places.name: Bandelier National Monument
places.description: Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings built into canyon walls, with trails combining archaeology and dramatic canyon scenery.
places.tip: Some dwellings require climbing wooden ladders — come prepared for light scrambling.

places.name: Old Guano Trail, Carlsbad
places.description: A 3-hour aboveground desert hike near the caverns, with Chihuahuan Desert views, wildflowers, and wildlife most cave-focused visitors skip entirely.
places.tip: Best hiked December-May to avoid the worst desert heat.

places.name: Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks National Monument
places.description: Jagged mountain spires rising straight from desert grassland, with hiking, wildlife viewing, and layered cultural history.
places.tip: A good stop between White Sands and points south.

places.name: Valley of Fires Recreation Area
places.description: Walk directly on ancient lava flows — an unusual and easy volcanic landscape most Southwest itineraries miss entirely.
places.tip: The paved nature trail makes this accessible even for a short stop.

places.name: Santa Fe
places.description: The oldest capital city in the US, with a historic Plaza, Canyon Road galleries, the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum, and some of the best New Mexican food anywhere.
places.tip: A genuine food destination in its own right — plan time to eat, not just sightsee.

places.name: Taos
places.description: Smaller and more scenic than Santa Fe, with strong Pueblo and art-colony history.
places.tip: Taos Pueblo itself is a living UNESCO World Heritage community — check visiting protocols before you go.

places.name: Albuquerque
places.description: The state's largest city and best logistical hub — a practical base for reaching the rest of the state.
places.tip: Old Town and the Sandia Peak Tramway are worth a stop even on a logistics-focused visit.

places.name: Chaco Culture National Historical Park
places.description: One of the most remote and historically significant Ancestral Puebloan sites in the Southwest — extensive ruins with real archaeological weight.
places.tip: Genuinely remote — check road conditions and fuel up before heading in.

places.name: Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge
places.description: A birdwatcher's haven — thousands of sandhill cranes and snow geese flock here during winter migration.
places.tip: Winter mornings and evenings are peak wildlife-viewing windows.

places.name: Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness
places.description: Alien-looking badlands with hoodoos and rock formations found almost nowhere else, in remote northwest New Mexico near Farmington.
places.tip: No marked trails — bring a GPS or offline map, and plenty of water.

places.name: Valley of Dreams
places.description: A lesser-known badlands formation near Bisti with striking rock formations and virtually no crowds.
places.tip: Combine with a Bisti visit for a full remote-badlands day.

places.name: Chimayó
places.description: A small northern New Mexico village famous for its distinctive red chile and El Santuario de Chimayó, a historic pilgrimage site.
places.tip: A worthwhile detour off the main Santa Fe-Taos corridor.

places.name: Bottomless Lakes State Park
places.description: A series of small, deep, spring-fed lakes near Roswell — a quiet, little-known stop on the eastern side of the state.
places.tip: A good rest stop on the drive between White Sands and Carlsbad.

places.name: "Red or green?"
places.description: New Mexico's official state question since 1999 — whether you want red (sweeter, dried, ripened) or green (bolder, fresher) chile on your dish. Order 'Christmas' for both.

places.name: Hatch green chile
places.description: Grown in the Hatch Valley and harvested in late summer — the backbone of New Mexican cuisine, roasted and folded into everything from cheeseburgers to breakfast burritos.

places.name: Chimayó red chile
places.description: A regional variety prized for its earthy, complex depth — the northern New Mexico counterpart to Hatch green chile, used in stews and enchiladas.

places.name: The Three Sisters & Pueblo food heritage
places.description: Corn, beans, and squash grown together, an agricultural tradition from the region's Pueblo peoples that still underpins New Mexican cooking today.

places.name: Posole & sopaipilla
places.description: Posole (hominy, treated dried corn) reflects Indigenous tradition; the pillowy fried sopaipilla shows the Spanish contribution of wheat flour.

places.name: Hatch Chile Festival
places.description: Held annually over Labor Day weekend in the small town of Hatch, drawing up to 30,000 visitors to a town of 1,600 for chile, food, and music.

name: New York
hero_tagline: The city that never sleeps, three hours from mountains that never crowd
hero_description: Everyone knows Manhattan — fewer know that upstate New York holds genuine wilderness in the Adirondacks and Catskills, waterfalls, and small towns a world away from Times Square.
best_time_to_visit: April-June and September-October for mild weather, fewer crowds, and (in fall) some of the best foliage in the Northeast. Winter is beautiful upstate for skiing but many mountain roads and trails become weather-dependent.
altitude_or_climate_note: NYC and upstate New York are essentially two different climates and two different trips — don't assume weather or crowd patterns from one apply to the other.
permits_note: Sam's Point in the Catskills requires reservations for parking May-October due to limited space. No general park entry fees for most Adirondack/Catskill state land, unlike Western national parks.
gear_note: Sturdy footwear for wet, rocky Catskills trails (several involve stream crossings or ladder scrambles). A NYC subway map app is more useful than a car in Manhattan itself.

places.name: Kaaterskill Falls
places.description: New York's tallest cascading waterfall at 260 ft, reached via a short but steep half-mile hike — the classic Catskills hike, especially dramatic during spring snowmelt.
places.tip: New viewing platform makes it safer than the old approach; still get there early to avoid crowds.

places.name: Sam's Point & Verkeerderkill Falls
places.description: A 7.5-mile out-and-back in Minnewaska State Park combining sweeping western views, a 180-ft waterfall, wooden ladder scrambles, and genuine ice caves you can walk through even in summer.
places.tip: Parking reservations required May-October — book ahead.

places.name: Giant Ledge
places.description: A steady climb through tall trees to open rock ledges with sweeping Catskills mountain views — a favorite among regular hikers.
places.tip: Moderately tough but manageable for a fit day hiker.

places.name: Catskills Scenic Byway
places.description: Winding mountain roads through the birthplace of the Hudson River School of painting, passing Kaaterskill Falls and the Five State Lookout (NY, NJ, PA, CT, MA all visible).
places.tip: A worthwhile drive even without stopping for every hike along the way.

places.name: Adirondack Park lakes
places.description: Paddle the Adirondacks' countless lakes, scuba dive shipwrecks in the St. Lawrence River, or take a gondola ride at Gore Mountain — the largest park in the contiguous US, bigger than Yellowstone.
places.tip: Lake Placid is a good, well-equipped base for exploring.

places.name: High Line
places.description: An elevated former rail line turned public walkway through Manhattan, with public art and Hudson River views threading between neighborhoods.
places.tip: Enter near Hudson Yards and walk south toward Chelsea Market for a natural half-day route.

places.name: Times Square & Broadway
places.description: The city's beating tourist heart — dazzling lights, and same-week discount tickets available for world-class theater.
places.tip: Check TKTS booths for last-minute discounted Broadway tickets.

places.name: Statue of Liberty & Ellis Island
places.description: A ferry from Battery Park reaches both — a symbol of freedom and the immigration history that shaped the city.
places.tip: Book ferry tickets ahead; lines at the dock can be long same-day.

places.name: Central Park
places.description: An 843-acre green escape in the middle of Manhattan — Strawberry Fields, Bow Bridge, and Bethesda Terrace are the classic stops.
places.tip: Rent a bike to cover more ground than walking allows.

places.name: The Met & MoMA
places.description: Two of the world's great art museums, a short distance apart — the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Modern Art.
places.tip: Both are large enough to need focus — pick a few galleries rather than trying to see everything.

places.name: Brooklyn Bridge
places.description: A walk across one of the city's most iconic structures, with skyline views back toward Manhattan.
places.tip: Morning light and thinner crowds make for the best photos and easiest walking.

places.name: Plattekill Falls
places.description: A short, somewhat steep hike to a secluded Catskills waterfall — far quieter than Kaaterskill Falls nearby.
places.tip: Good for photography and quiet reflection away from the crowds.

places.name: Diamond Notch Falls
places.description: A waterfall near Hunter with a genuine swimming hole at its base — a local favorite for cooling off in summer.
places.tip: Less crowded than the marquee Catskills waterfalls.

places.name: Olana State Historic Site
places.description: The Persian-inspired home of Hudson River School painter Frederic Church, with some of the best scenic overlooks in the Hudson Valley.
places.tip: A genuine hidden-gem photo spot most upstate itineraries skip.

places.name: Esopus & Willowemoc Creeks
places.description: Renowned fly-fishing streams in the Catskills, quiet and scenic even if you don't fish.
places.tip: A peaceful stop for a picnic or short streamside walk.

places.name: Livingston Manor
places.description: A small Catskills town with genuine small-town charm, well outside the more touristy Hunter/Woodstock circuit.
places.tip: A good base for a quieter, less crowded Catskills trip.

places.name: New York-style pizza
places.description: Thin, foldable, hand-tossed slices — an institution since Lombardi's opened the city's first pizzeria in 1905.

places.name: New York bagels
places.description: Boiled then baked for a chewy interior and crisp exterior — classically topped with lox, cream cheese, and capers, rooted in the city's Jewish deli tradition.

places.name: Pastrami sandwich (Katz's Delicatessen)
places.description: Piled-high pastrami on rye at one of the city's most famous and historic delis, on Manhattan's Lower East Side.

places.name: Broadway theater
places.description: World-class musicals and plays in the Theater District, often performed by internationally known actors and musicians.

places.name: Neighborhood food cultures
places.description: Chinatown's dim sum, Little Italy, and Harlem's jazz-era food and music traditions all sit within walking distance of each other — the city's diversity is itself the draw.

name: Michigan
hero_tagline: The only state bordering four Great Lakes, and a coney dog that will not be confused with Chicago's
hero_description: Towering sand dunes on freshwater coastline that looks Caribbean-clear, an island where cars have been banned for over a century, and a food culture shaped by mining immigrants and auto-factory workers alike.
best_time_to_visit: June-August for warm weather and full beach/dune access. Fall brings excellent foliage; winter turns the state into a serious snow-sports destination, especially the Upper Peninsula.
altitude_or_climate_note: Michigan is really two states in one — the Lower Peninsula's beaches and cherry country, and the far more rugged, remote Upper Peninsula across the Mackinac Bridge.
permits_note: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore requires a park pass (weekly or annual). Mackinac Island bans private cars entirely — walk, bike, or take a horse-drawn carriage.
gear_note: Water and sun protection for dune hiking — sand hikes at Sleeping Bear or Warren Dunes are more strenuous than they look. A reliable eSIM or offline maps for remote Upper Peninsula trips.

places.name: Pierce Stocking Scenic Drive
places.description: A drive through Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore to the Lake Michigan Overlook, 450 ft above the water — one of the best views in the Midwest.
places.tip: Pair with the Empire Bluff Trail for a less-crowded alternative viewpoint.

places.name: Dune Climb, Sleeping Bear Dunes
places.description: A genuine workout disguised as fun — climb the massive dune slope for panoramic Lake Michigan views most visitors underestimate.
places.tip: Go in cooler morning hours; the sand gets brutally hot by midday.

places.name: Mackinac Island
places.description: An entire island where cars have been banned for over a century — horse-drawn carriages and bicycles only, with a genuinely frozen-in-time atmosphere.
places.tip: Rent a bike to circle the island's perimeter road for the full experience.

places.name: Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore
places.description: Dramatic multicolored sandstone cliffs along Lake Superior in the Upper Peninsula — best seen by kayak or boat tour right along the cliff base.
places.tip: The Upper Peninsula is remote — plan fuel and supply stops carefully.

places.name: M-22 Scenic Highway
places.description: A coastal route along Lake Michigan's Leelanau and Benzie counties, threading wineries, farm stands, and small fishing towns.
places.tip: Stop in Leland's Fishtown, a cluster of historic fishing shanties worth 30 minutes.

places.name: North Country National Scenic Trail
places.description: Michigan holds a quarter of this 4,600-mile trail, the longest in the National Trail System once completed — accessible in short, scenic sections without needing to hike the whole thing.
places.tip: Pick a local trailhead section rather than attempting the full route.

places.name: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore
places.description: 35 miles of Lake Michigan shoreline and towering dunes — the signature natural attraction of the state.
places.tip: A weekly park pass is required; buy ahead to skip the gate line.

places.name: Mackinac Bridge
