places.description: The bridge connecting Michigan's two peninsulas — a five-mile suspension bridge and a genuine engineering landmark in its own right.
places.tip: Stop at the Bridge View Park on either side for the best photos.

places.name: Traverse City
places.description: The hub of Michigan's cherry country and a good base for exploring the Leelanau Peninsula's wineries and Sleeping Bear Dunes.
places.tip: Visit July-August for peak fresh cherry season.

places.name: Detroit Riverwalk
places.description: A revitalized waterfront path along the Detroit River, part of the city's broader downtown resurgence.
places.tip: Pair with a coney dog stop at one of the historic downtown Coney Islands.

places.name: Silver Lake Sand Dunes
places.description: A lesser-known dune system offering ORV riding alongside quieter, more secluded hiking areas than the busier Sleeping Bear Dunes.
places.tip: A good alternative if Sleeping Bear feels too crowded in peak summer.

places.name: Warren Dunes & Tower Hill
places.description: A 260-ft dune climb rewarding a breathtaking view, in a state park with a quieter feel than the more famous northern dune systems.
places.tip: Good for a day trip from Chicago or southwest Michigan.

places.name: Upper Peninsula waterfalls
places.description: Over 130 documented waterfalls scattered across the UP — genuinely remote, uncrowded hiking most Lower Peninsula visitors never see.
places.tip: Pick a cluster near one town rather than trying to chase waterfalls across the whole UP.

places.name: P.J. Hoffmaster State Park
places.description: An interpretive dune center near Muskegon telling Michigan's unique sand dune ecology story, with hiking trails through wooded dunes.
places.tip: A good educational stop if traveling with kids.

places.name: Arcadia Scenic Turnout
places.description: A quick M-22 stop with 120 steps up to a Lake Michigan overlook — a fast, low-effort payoff most drive-through visitors skip.
places.tip: Good for a short break if you don't have time for a full dune hike.

places.name: Detroit-style Coney dog
places.description: A natural-casing hot dog topped with beanless meat chili, mustard, and onions — no ketchup, ever. Distinct from Chicago-style hot dogs.

places.name: Upper Peninsula pasties
places.description: Savory hand pies of beef, potato, onion, and rutabaga, brought by 19th-century Cornish miners as portable meals for long shifts underground.

places.name: Detroit-style pizza
places.description: Square-cut, thick and airy crust with caramelized cheese edges, baked in steel pans originally used for auto-factory parts.

places.name: Traverse City tart cherries
places.description: Michigan is a top US tart cherry producer, thanks to Lake Michigan's moderating effect on the orchards — fresh in July-August, in pies and wine year-round.

places.name: Motown
places.description: Detroit's music legacy as the birthplace of the Motown sound, a defining piece of the city's cultural identity.

places.name: Mackinac Island fudge
places.description: A tourist tradition dating back generations, made fresh on marble slabs in shops across the car-free island.

name: Florida
hero_tagline: A subtropical wilderness, a string of islands, and a Cuban sandwich that settles arguments
hero_description: The Everglades' 'river of grass' is a UNESCO World Heritage Site most visitors never see beyond the highway — and the Keys, Miami's Cuban food culture, and the beaches are only part of the story.
best_time_to_visit: December-April — Florida's dry season, with lower humidity, fewer mosquitoes, and much more comfortable Everglades hiking. Stone crab season (mid-October to May 1) overlaps nicely with this window. Avoid June-November if possible: hurricane season, heat, and humidity all peak.
altitude_or_climate_note: Hot and humid most of the year, with a real hurricane risk June-November — check storm forecasts before any summer or fall trip. The Everglades are also buggiest and least comfortable in wet season (roughly May-October).
permits_note: Everglades National Park charges a per-vehicle entrance fee (around $30). No special permits needed for the Keys' public sites; some backcountry camping in the Everglades requires a permit.
gear_note: Insect repellent is non-negotiable in the Everglades, especially wet season. Reef-safe sunscreen and water shoes for the Keys' rocky shorelines and coral-adjacent snorkeling.

places.name: Anhinga Trail
places.description: A half-mile boardwalk through Everglades wetlands with genuinely excellent wildlife viewing — alligators, herons, and dozens of bird species close enough to feel real.
places.tip: An easy, family-friendly entry point to the park that still delivers on wildlife.

places.name: Shark Valley
places.description: A 15-mile paved loop through the Everglades, walkable, bikeable, or via tram tour, ending at a 65-ft observation tower with sweeping sawgrass views.
places.tip: Rent a bike for a good middle-ground pace between walking and the tram.

places.name: Tamiami Trail through Big Cypress
places.description: A scenic drive through Big Cypress National Preserve with an expansive canopy of cypress trees, especially striking during rainy season.
places.tip: A good way to see Everglades-adjacent wilderness without leaving your car.

places.name: Florida Keys road trip (Overseas Highway)
places.description: The classic drive from Miami to Key West, island-hopping over open water on one of the most scenic roads in the country.
places.tip: Give yourself more than a day — the Keys reward a slow pace, not a straight shot to Key West.

places.name: Kayaking the Ten Thousand Islands
places.description: A maze of mangrove islands on the Everglades' Gulf Coast side — quiet paddling with real odds of spotting manatees and dolphins.
places.tip: Go with a guide unless you're experienced with mangrove navigation — it's easy to get turned around.

places.name: Blue Hole, Big Pine Key
places.description: A former quarry turned freshwater oasis in the Lower Keys, with real odds of spotting alligators, turtles, and birds from marked viewing areas.
places.tip: Pair with the adjacent National Key Deer Refuge.

places.name: Everglades National Park
places.description: The largest subtropical wilderness in the US and a UNESCO World Heritage Site — mangrove forests, cypress domes, and sawgrass prairie found nowhere else in the country.
places.tip: Visit dry season (December-April) for far better comfort and wildlife visibility.

places.name: Key West
places.description: The southernmost point in the continental US — Duval Street, sunset celebrations at Mallory Square, and a genuinely distinct island atmosphere.
places.tip: Sunset at Mallory Square is a nightly ritual worth planning around.

places.name: South Beach & Little Havana, Miami
places.description: Miami's iconic Art Deco beachfront alongside the Cuban cultural heart of the city — two completely different Miami experiences within a short drive.
places.tip: A Little Havana food walking tour is a good way to get oriented before exploring on your own.

places.name: Walt Disney World & Universal Orlando
places.description: The theme park capital of the world — a very different kind of Florida trip from the Everglades or Keys.
places.tip: Book ride reservations and park tickets well in advance during peak seasons.

places.name: Indian Key Historic State Park
places.description: An uninhabited island near Islamorada with a fascinating 1800s shipwreck-salvage history, accessible only by boat or kayak.
places.tip: The boat-only access keeps it genuinely quiet compared to roadside Keys attractions.

places.name: Everglades City
places.description: A small, authentic gateway town on the Everglades' Gulf side, known for genuinely local seafood away from the Miami-side crowds.
places.tip: A good base for Ten Thousand Islands kayaking and stone crab in season.

places.name: Mahogany Hammock
places.description: A boardwalk loop through a dense hardwood hammock — a distinctly different Everglades ecosystem from the open sawgrass prairie most visitors picture.
places.tip: A quick, easy stop that shows a side of the Everglades most itineraries skip.

places.name: Pa-hay-okee Overlook
places.description: A short boardwalk to a wide sawgrass prairie view — one of the best photo spots in the park, with a fraction of Anhinga Trail's crowds.
places.tip: Good for sunset given the open, unobstructed sightlines.

places.name: Stone crab claws
places.description: Florida's real signature dish, in season mid-October through May — only the claws are harvested, and the crab is returned to the sea to regrow them.

places.name: Cuban sandwich
places.description: Roast pork, ham, Swiss cheese, pickles, and mustard on pressed crispy bread — Miami's most iconic handheld food, rooted in Key West and Tampa's Cuban immigrant communities.

places.name: Little Havana
places.description: Miami's Cuban-American cultural heart — ventanita coffee windows, cigar shops, and late-night Cuban food that runs well past midnight.

places.name: Key lime pie
places.description: Florida's official state pie — key lime juice, egg yolks, and sweetened condensed milk in a graham cracker crust, found statewide despite the name.

places.name: Pastelitos & croquetas
places.description: Cuban-American bakery staples — flaky glazed pastries and savory ham croquettes, a daily ritual at Miami's countless local bakeries.

name: Texas
hero_tagline: Big enough to hold a desert national park, wine country, and three distinct barbecue traditions
hero_description: The Lone Star State is genuinely its own country's worth of terrain — West Texas desert canyons, Hill Country rivers and vineyards, and a barbecue culture with real regional rivalries most visitors never realize exist.
best_time_to_visit: Spring (March-April) for wildflowers — bluebonnets carpet the Hill Country roadsides — and fall (October-November) for milder temperatures statewide. Summer is genuinely brutal, especially in Big Bend's low desert.
altitude_or_climate_note: Texas is too big for one weather pattern — Big Bend's desert heat, Hill Country's river-valley humidity, and the Gulf Coast's tropical air can all be happening at once. Check conditions for your specific region, not the state as a whole.
permits_note: Hamilton Pool Preserve near Austin requires a reservation. Big Bend is remote — fuel up before entering, services inside the park are limited.
gear_note: Water, water, and more water for Big Bend hiking — heat exhaustion is a real risk. Cell service is unreliable in both Big Bend and remote Hill Country — download offline maps first.

places.name: Lost Mine Trail, Big Bend
places.description: A moderately strenuous hike with some of the best payoff views in the park — genuinely divisive online (some call it overrated, most call it a must-do), best hiked when the trail is quiet.
places.tip: Go early morning to avoid both heat and crowds on this popular trail.

places.name: Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive
places.description: Big Bend's signature drive, passing Mule Ears Viewpoint and ending near Santa Elena Canyon, with short hikes branching off along the way.
places.tip: Stop at the free Fossil Discovery Exhibit near Panther Junction on the way in.

places.name: Twisted Sisters (FM 335/336/337)
places.description: Over 100 miles of sharp turns, steep hills, and river crossings through the Hill Country — a favorite for both drivers and motorcyclists.
places.tip: Spring wildflowers and fall foliage both make this drive worth timing around.

places.name: Gorman Falls, Colorado Bend State Park
places.description: A 3-mile moderate hike to a 70-ft waterfall that feels completely out of place in the Hill Country's otherwise dry, desert-esque terrain.
places.tip: The fragile ecosystem means you'll view the falls from a distance rather than swim in them.

places.name: Emory Peak, Big Bend
places.description: A strenuous 5-6 hour hike to the highest point in the Chisos Mountains, with real odds of spotting black bears.
places.tip: Start very early — this is a full-day commitment, not a quick summit.

places.name: Hamilton Pool Preserve
places.description: A collapsed grotto with a waterfall feeding a jade-green swimming hole, about 45 minutes from Austin.
places.tip: Reservations required — this isn't a walk-up spot.

places.name: The Alamo, San Antonio
places.description: The historic mission and fortress at the center of the 1836 Battle of the Alamo — Texas's most visited historic landmark.
places.tip: Pair with a walk along the River Walk right next door.

places.name: River Walk, San Antonio
places.description: A network of walkways along the San Antonio River lined with restaurants and shops, below street level in the city center.
places.tip: Evening is especially atmospheric, with restaurant lights reflecting off the water.

places.name: Austin
places.description: The state capital and a genuine live-music and food capital, with a laid-back, outdoorsy energy distinct from Texas's other big cities.
places.tip: Time a visit around SXSW (March) or ACL Fest (October) if festivals interest you — otherwise avoid those weeks for lodging prices.

places.name: Big Bend National Park
places.description: One of the most remote national parks in the country, with the Rio Grande, desert canyons, and the Chisos Mountains all in one place.
places.tip: Plan at least two days — a single day only scratches the surface of the park's range of ecosystems.

places.name: Marfa
places.description: A tiny West Texas art town known for minimalist installations and the unexplained Marfa Lights phenomenon — an unlikely cultural outpost in the middle of the desert.
places.tip: A good stop on the way to or from Big Bend.

places.name: Enchanted Rock
places.description: A massive pink granite dome near Fredericksburg with a moderate summit hike and sweeping Hill Country views.
places.tip: About 90 minutes from Austin — a good half-day trip.

places.name: Caddo Lake
places.description: A cypress-swamp lake on the Texas-Louisiana border, moody and atmospheric — genuinely unlike anywhere else in the state.
places.tip: A kayak or guided boat tour is the best way to experience the cypress groves.

places.name: Palo Duro Canyon
places.description: The second-largest canyon in the US, in the Texas Panhandle — a genuine surprise most visitors don't associate with flat West Texas plains.
places.tip: Far less crowded than Big Bend despite comparable scenery.

places.name: Terlingua Ghost Town
places.description: A former mercury-mining town turned quirky community right at Big Bend's doorstep — porch-sitting at the Starlight Theatre is a genuine local ritual.
places.tip: A good place to grab dinner after a day in the park.

places.name: Central Texas brisket
places.description: Slow-smoked over post oak, the centerpiece of Texas barbecue — order by the pound, not by the plate, at Lockhart's historic meat markets.

places.name: Three regional BBQ styles
places.description: Central Texas (dry-rubbed brisket, German/Czech meat-market roots), East Texas (sweeter, tomato-based sauce, Southern influence), and South Texas barbacoa (whole cow heads slow-cooked in underground pits, a Spanish/Mexican ranching tradition).

places.name: Tex-Mex
places.description: Not Mexican food, and doesn't claim to be — a distinct border cuisine (queso, cheese enchiladas, fajitas, puffy tacos) that originated with Tejano home cooking.

places.name: Breakfast tacos
places.description: Austin's unofficial civic religion — the Austin-vs-San Antonio, flour-vs-corn debate is Texas's most heated (and good-natured) culinary argument.

places.name: Ranch Water & sweet tea
places.description: Ranch Water (tequila, Topo Chico, lime) is the unofficial drink of Texas summers; sweet tea, brewed strong over ice, is treated as heritage more than beverage.

places.name: Live music heritage
places.description: Austin's honky-tonks (Broken Spoke since 1964) and blues clubs (Antone's) alongside SXSW and ACL Fest anchor the state's reputation as a live-music powerhouse.

name: Hawaii
hero_tagline: Six islands, six completely different personalities, and a live volcano you can check on before you go
hero_description: From Kauai's knife-edge cliffs to the Big Island's active lava fields, Hawaii isn't one tropical vacation repeated six times — each island has a genuinely distinct character, and the culture runs far deeper than the beach.
best_time_to_visit: April-May and September-November for lower prices and fewer crowds than the winter high season (December-March). Hawaii sits in the Pacific hurricane belt — storms are possible June-November, with 2026 seeing real activity (Hurricane Lala and Tropical Storm Moke both affected the islands that August), so check forecasts for late-summer trips.
altitude_or_climate_note: Kilauea volcano has been in active episodic eruption since December 2024, with no fixed schedule — individual episodes last hours, not weeks. Check the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory status page the morning of any Volcanoes National Park visit.
permits_note: Nāpali Coast (Kauai) hiking permits are required beyond Hanakāpīʻai Falls and sell out fast — book well ahead. Haleakalā sunrise viewing (Maui) requires a separate reservation.
gear_note: Reef-safe sunscreen is required by law in Hawaii to protect coral reefs. Sturdy shoes for lava-field hiking on the Big Island — the terrain is genuinely sharp and uneven, not sandal-friendly.

places.name: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park
places.description: The Big Island's most-visited attraction — lava tubes, steaming craters, and (episodically, since December 2024) an active eruption inside Halemaʻumaʻu crater.
places.tip: Check the USGS status page the morning you go — there's no eruption schedule to plan around.

places.name: Chain of Craters Road
places.description: An 18.8-mile descent through Hawaii Volcanoes National Park ending at lava flows that once covered the road, with numerous crater overlooks along the way.
places.tip: Bring water, snacks, and sun protection — services are minimal along the route.

places.name: Nāpali Coast
places.description: Kauai's most dramatic coastline — knife-edge cliffs dropping straight into the Pacific, hikeable via the Kalalau Trail or viewable by boat.
places.tip: Permits for anything past Hanakāpīʻai Falls sell out fast — book as early as possible.

places.name: Road to Hana
places.description: Maui's legendary drive — 620-plus curves and 59 bridges past waterfalls, black sand beaches, and rainforest, genuinely earning its reputation as a full-day experience.
places.tip: Start early and don't rush — the stops are the entire point of the drive.

places.name: Kilauea Iki Crater hike
places.description: A 4-mile hike descending into and crossing a solidified lava lake — one of the most memorable short hikes in any US national park.
places.tip: Can also be done as a brief viewing stop from the rim if you're short on time.

places.name: Mauna Kea summit stargazing
places.description: One of the best stargazing locations on Earth, at nearly 14,000 ft — request a summit tour or visit the Visitor Information Station for acclimatization first.
places.tip: Altitude sickness is a real risk — spend time at the visitor station before continuing to the summit.

places.name: Waikiki Beach, Oahu
places.description: Hawaii's most famous beach and the heart of Honolulu's resort district — urban energy paired directly with the ocean.
places.tip: Diamond Head crater hike is a short trip from Waikiki if you want a morning workout before the beach.

places.name: North Shore, Oahu
places.description: The legendary surf culture coast — massive winter waves, food trucks, and a slower pace than Waikiki.
places.tip: Winter (November-February) brings the biggest, most famous surf; summer is calmer and better for swimming.

places.name: Haleakalā National Park
places.description: Maui's dormant volcano summit, famous for sunrise views above the clouds.
places.tip: Sunrise viewing requires its own separate reservation, booked ahead.

places.name: Waimea Canyon, Kauai
places.description: Called the 'Grand Canyon of the Pacific' — red-and-green layered cliffs accessible by an easy scenic drive with multiple overlooks.
places.tip: Combine with a Nāpali Coast boat tour for the island's two signature views in one day.

places.name: Makalawena Beach
places.description: A pristine white-sand Big Island beach reached via a short hike over a lava field — a fraction of the crowds of the resort-adjacent beaches.
places.tip: No facilities — bring your own water and shade.

places.name: Holualoa (Big Island) / Kula (Maui)
places.description: Cooler-climate upcountry towns with rolling farmland and local coffee and lavender farms — a genuinely different Hawaii than the coastal resorts.
places.tip: Ali'i Kula Lavender Farm on Maui is a quiet, unexpected stop.

places.name: Byodo-In Temple, Oahu
places.description: A stunning replica of a 950-year-old Japanese temple tucked into the Valley of the Temples on Oahu's windward side.
places.tip: A quiet, contemplative stop most Waikiki-based visitors never make it to.

places.name: Petroglyph Park, Big Island
places.description: Ancient Hawaiian rock carvings alongside the historic Ala Kahakai Trail, a 175-mile corridor connecting hundreds of traditional settlement sites.
places.tip: Combine with Puʻukoholā Heiau, about 20 minutes north.

places.name: Poke
places.description: Cubed raw fish marinated with limu seaweed, onion, and Hawaiian salt — a Hawaiian word meaning 'cut into chunks,' now globally trendy but still best had fresh on the islands.

places.name: Lūʻau
places.description: A traditional feast rooted in the word 'ahaʻaina,' centered on a kalua pig cooked in an underground imu oven, accompanied by hula, chant, and live music.

places.name: Plate lunch
places.description: A local staple reflecting Hawaii's plantation-era immigrant mix — typically a protein, rice, and macaroni salad, found at unpretentious lunch counters across the islands.

places.name: Aloha spirit
places.description: More than a greeting — a cultural value of mutual respect, care, and hospitality that shapes how locals expect visitors to treat both people and land.

places.name: Hula
places.description: Ranges from hula kahiko (ancient, chant-accompanied) to hula 'auana (modern, ukulele and guitar) — a storytelling art form, not just entertainment.

name: South Dakota
hero_tagline: Granite presidents, an ancient seabed turned badlands, and a bar snack invented by homesick pioneers
hero_description: The Black Hills pack granite spires, cave systems, and free-roaming bison into a compact, drivable area — with the otherworldly Badlands and deep Lakota history rounding out a state most people fly over.
best_time_to_visit: September is the sweet spot — warm days, cool nights, thinner crowds, lower prices, fall color, and the Custer State Park Buffalo Roundup in late September. Avoid the first two weeks of August if crowds aren't your thing: the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally brings roughly half a million riders to the region and books out lodging for a wide radius.
altitude_or_climate_note: The Black Hills and Badlands are a genuine four-season destination, but conditions swing hard — summer highs in the 70s-90s with full services, versus a beautiful but much quieter winter with some roads and cave tours on reduced schedules.
permits_note: No park entrance fee for Badlands is required beyond the standard NPS pass. Wind Cave and Jewel Cave tours run on a full schedule only in summer — check hours before planning around a specific cave tour in shoulder season.
gear_note: Layers for the day-to-night temperature swing at elevation in the Black Hills. Sun protection for the Badlands, which offer little natural shade on most trails.

places.name: Needles Highway & Iron Mountain Road
places.description: Engineering marvels through granite — sharp switchbacks, pigtail bridges, and narrow tunnels framing Mount Rushmore from a distance.
places.tip: Not suited for large RVs — the tunnels are genuinely narrow.

places.name: Badlands Loop Road
places.description: A scenic byway through Badlands National Park's otherworldly eroded formations, with 12 overlooks and access to hiking trails along the way.
places.tip: Once an ancient seabed, the park is also one of the richest fossil beds in the world.

places.name: Sunday Gulch Trail, Sylvan Lake
places.description: The best hike in the Black Hills according to locals — a rugged trail through a granite gulch starting from the 'Crown Jewel' Sylvan Lake.
places.tip: Rent a kayak at Sylvan Lake afterward to cool off.

places.name: Wildlife Loop Road, Custer State Park
places.description: A drive through rolling prairie with excellent odds of encountering free-roaming bison herds, along with pronghorn and prairie dogs.
places.tip: Early morning or evening gives the best wildlife activity.

places.name: Spearfish Canyon Scenic Byway
places.description: Towering limestone canyon walls and cascading waterfalls in the northern Black Hills — Roughlock Falls is the classic stop.
places.tip: A quieter, less-visited corner of the Black Hills than the Rushmore area.

places.name: Wind Cave & Jewel Cave
places.description: Two of the longest cave systems in the world, both offering ranger-led tours — genuinely different experiences worth doing both.
places.tip: Combine with above-ground hiking at Wind Cave National Park while waiting for your tour slot.

places.name: Mount Rushmore
places.description: The iconic granite presidential carving and South Dakota's most visited attraction, with an evening lighting ceremony in summer.
places.tip: Stick around for the lighting ceremony if visiting in peak season.

places.name: Badlands National Park
places.description: Dramatic striped rock formations across a former ancient seabed — one of the most visually distinct national parks in the country.
places.tip: Many visitors' favorite single stop in the whole state.

places.name: Crazy Horse Memorial
places.description: An in-progress mountain carving honoring Lakota leader Crazy Horse — significantly larger in scale than Mount Rushmore, with a museum on Native American history and culture.
places.tip: The visitor center's Native American exhibits are worth real time, not just a photo stop.

places.name: Custer State Park
places.description: The centerpiece of the Black Hills — Sylvan Lake, the Wildlife Loop, and some of the region's best hiking, all in one park.
places.tip: Easily worth a full day or more on its own.

places.name: Eleventh Hour Gulch Trail
places.description: An unmaintained, off-the-radar scramble up boulders and ladders near Spearfish Canyon, ending at a golden-hour view over the canyon.
places.tip: Not officially managed — go prepared and expect a rougher trail than marked hikes.

places.name: Community Caves Trail
places.description: A short, steep roadside hike to small caves overlooking Spearfish Canyon — good for photos and spotting nesting birds.
places.tip: Also unmaintained — a genuine local secret, not in most guidebooks.

places.name: Delta-01 Launch Control Facility
places.description: A preserved Cold War-era Minuteman missile launch control center, part of Minuteman Missile National Historic Site — an unexpectedly compelling stop most Black Hills itineraries skip.
places.tip: Advance reservations recommended for the underground tour.

places.name: Mammoth Site, Hot Springs
places.description: An active paleontological dig site where mammoth fossils are still being excavated in place — genuinely unique among South Dakota's attractions.
places.tip: Pair with a Wind Cave tour and Hot Springs town visit for a full day.

places.name: Chapel in the Hills
places.description: A replica of Norway's Borgund stave church tucked into the Black Hills — a quiet, unexpected architectural stop.
places.tip: Free to visit and rarely crowded.

places.name: Chislic
places.description: Deep-fried cubed meat (traditionally mutton, now often beef or lamb) served with salt and saltines — invented by Russian-German pioneers in Hutchinson County in the 1870s to use up tougher, older sheep.

places.name: Kuchen
places.description: South Dakota's official state dessert since 1988 — a German fruit-filled pastry with a thick shortbread crust, reflecting the state's German-Russian immigrant heritage.

places.name: Lakota foodways
places.description: Wasna (pounded dried buffalo, cranberries, and grain), wojapi (berry sauce), and pemmican reflect Lakota Sioux tradition — bison historically provided meat, hide, and tools for the Great Plains tribes.

places.name: Frybread
places.description: A Native American staple flatbread, often topped with beef, cheese, and vegetables — available at eateries near Crazy Horse Memorial and across the state.

places.name: Sturgis Motorcycle Rally
places.description: Held annually in early August, drawing roughly half a million riders — transforms the region's food scene for the week with buffalo burgers and vendor food lining the streets.

name: Georgia
hero_tagline: Cobblestone coastal charm in the south, Appalachian waterfalls in the north
hero_description: Savannah's Spanish-moss squares and wild-horse barrier islands sit a few hours from Blue Ridge waterfall hikes and mountain wine country — two very different Georgias, both genuinely worth the trip.
best_time_to_visit: Spring (March-May) for mild coastal weather and blooming azaleas in Savannah, or fall (October-November) for Blue Ridge foliage and grape-harvest wine country. Summer is hot and humid statewide, especially on the coast.
altitude_or_climate_note: Coastal Georgia and the North Georgia mountains run on different climates — humid subtropical on the coast, cooler and more seasonal in the Blue Ridge foothills.
permits_note: No special permits for most state parks; Cumberland Island requires a ferry reservation and has a daily visitor cap, so book ahead.
gear_note: Insect repellent for coastal marsh areas. Layers for North Georgia mountain mornings even in warmer months.

places.name: Blue Ridge waterfall hikes
places.description: North Georgia's mountain town of Blue Ridge anchors a cluster of accessible waterfall trails, including the family-friendly Fall Branch Falls.
places.tip: Combine with the Blue Ridge Scenic Railway for a slower-paced day.

places.name: Cumberland Island
places.description: Georgia's wildest barrier island — wild horses, empty beaches, and the ruins of the Carnegie family's Dungeness mansion, reachable only by ferry.
places.tip: Daily visitor numbers are capped — book the ferry well ahead.

places.name: Appalachian Trail (Georgia section)
places.description: The southern terminus of the 2,190-mile Appalachian Trail starts here — day sections near Blue Ridge offer panoramic views without committing to a thru-hike.
places.tip: Blood Mountain, near Vogel State Park, is a popular day-hike section.

places.name: Tallulah Gorge State Park
places.description: One of the deepest gorges east of the Mississippi, with suspension bridge crossings and dramatic overlooks.
places.tip: Permits are required to hike to the gorge floor — check availability at the interpretive center.

places.name: Dahlonega wine country
places.description: North Georgia's wine trail, centered on Dahlonega's gold-rush history alongside family-owned vineyards and mountain overlooks.
places.tip: September-November brings harvest season and the best foliage backdrop.

places.name: Helen
places.description: An alpine Bavarian-style village in the North Georgia mountains, with river tubing, hiking, and an unlikely but genuine German cultural festival scene.
places.tip: Especially charming at Christmas, when the town leans fully into its Alpine theme.

places.name: Savannah Historic District
places.description: Cobblestone streets, Spanish-moss-draped squares, and antebellum architecture that make Savannah one of the most walkable historic cities in the South.
places.tip: Go early morning to have the famous squares mostly to yourself.

places.name: Atlanta
places.description: Georgia's capital and a genuine civil rights history hub, alongside the Georgia Aquarium, Ponce City Market, and a soul food scene locals fiercely defend.
places.tip: The BeltLine walking/biking path is a good way to see several neighborhoods at once.

places.name: Jekyll Island
places.description: A former Gilded Age retreat turned public barrier island, with historic mansions, beaches, and Driftwood Beach's iconic bleached tree skeletons.
places.tip: Driftwood Beach at sunrise is one of the most photographed spots on the Georgia coast.

places.name: Tybee Island
places.description: Savannah's closest beach getaway, with a historic lighthouse and an easygoing, low-key beach town feel.
places.tip: A convenient half-day add-on if you're based in Savannah.

places.name: Cloudland Canyon State Park
places.description: Dramatic canyon views and waterfall hikes in far northwest Georgia — a genuine alternative to the busier Blue Ridge trails.
places.tip: Less crowded than the North Georgia waterfall circuit near Blue Ridge.

places.name: Sapelo Island
places.description: A remote barrier island accessible only by ferry, home to the Gullah Geechee community of Hog Hammock — a rare, living piece of coastal Georgia's African American heritage.
places.tip: Ferry access is limited — check the schedule and reserve ahead.

places.name: Don Carter State Park
places.description: A quieter lake-based state park near Gainesville, with kayaking and hiking away from the more heavily trafficked North Georgia mountain trails.
places.tip: A good lower-key alternative when Blue Ridge feels too busy.

places.name: Wormsloe Historic Site
places.description: A mile-and-a-half oak-lined avenue leading to colonial ruins just outside Savannah — one of the most photographed, least crowded spots near the city.
places.tip: A quick, easy add-on to a Savannah day.

places.name: Providence Canyon State Park
places.description: Called Georgia's 'Little Grand Canyon' — colorful eroded gullies in the state's southwest corner, far off the typical Georgia tourist circuit.
places.tip: A genuine surprise for anyone who thinks Georgia is only coast and mountains.

places.name: Peaches
places.description: Georgia's identity fruit — woven into street names, state symbols, and menus statewide, well beyond the literal fruit stands.

places.name: Soul food
places.description: Fried chicken, collard greens, mac and cheese, and cornbread — Atlanta institutions like Busy Bee Cafe (since 1947) and Mary Mac's Tea Room (since 1945) treat recipes as generational heirlooms.

places.name: Lowcountry & Gullah Geechee coastal cooking
places.description: Savannah south through the Golden Isles, cuisine shifts toward shrimp, crab, oysters, and rice dishes shaped by Gullah Geechee coastal communities.

places.name: Brunswick stew
places.description: A tomato-based stew served with cornbread, especially associated with the coastal city of Brunswick and barbecue joints statewide.

places.name: Shrimp and grits
places.description: Ground corn grits topped with sautéed shrimp — a coastal Georgia staple bridging Lowcountry and soul food traditions.

name: Oregon
hero_tagline: The deepest lake in the country, a coastline built for road-tripping, and 80-plus breweries
hero_description: Crater Lake's impossibly blue caldera, sea-stack coastline, and a Portland food scene that treats farm-to-table as a founding principle, not a trend — Oregon rewards slow, deliberate exploration.
best_time_to_visit: Late June through September for the most reliable weather and full mountain-pass access — Crater Lake can still have snow into July. September is a local secret: summer weather often lingers with thinner crowds, and late October brings excellent foliage along the Columbia River Highway.
altitude_or_climate_note: Coastal mornings stay chilly even in July — pack a fleece regardless of season. The coast, Cascades, and high desert around Bend all run different weather patterns simultaneously.
permits_note: No general park entrance fee complications, but popular lodging (Cannon Beach, Bend, Crater Lake) sells out months ahead in summer — book early.
gear_note: Layers are non-negotiable — even peak summer days can end with a cold, foggy coastal evening. Good traction footwear for Cleetwood Cove Trail's steep return climb at Crater Lake.

places.name: Cleetwood Cove Trail, Crater Lake
places.description: The only legal access point down to the water's edge of Crater Lake — steep on the return climb, but the only way to actually touch the deepest lake in the US.
places.tip: Check the National Park Service website before your visit — this trail is seasonal.

places.name: Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor
places.description: The most dramatic hiking section of the Oregon Coast — surreal cliffs rising straight from the Pacific along a dedicated scenic corridor.
places.tip: Numerous pullouts let you sample short hikes without committing to the full corridor.

places.name: Tamolitch Blue Pool
places.description: A turquoise pool fed by an underground spring, reached via a 3.6-mile hike through old-growth forest in Willamette National Forest.
places.tip: The color is genuinely startling — bring a camera with a polarizing filter if you have one.

places.name: Columbia River Gorge & Multnomah Falls
places.description: Dramatic cliffs and waterfalls along the Historic Columbia River Highway, with Multnomah Falls as the tallest and most famous.
places.tip: Go early or on a weekday — this is one of the most visited spots in the state.

places.name: Wallowa Mountains
places.description: Alpine peaks, deep valleys, and gondola rides in far northeast Oregon — dubbed 'Oregon's Switzerland' and largely overlooked by coast-and-Portland itineraries.
places.tip: A genuine detour from the standard Oregon route, worth it for the solitude alone.

places.name: Garfield Peak, Crater Lake
places.description: A 3.3-mile roundtrip climbing over 1,000 ft for panoramic views beyond the lake itself.
places.tip: Watchman Peak (1.7 miles) is a gentler sunrise alternative with similarly excellent views.

places.name: Crater Lake National Park
places.description: Oregon's only national park — the deepest lake in the US, formed by the collapse of Mount Mazama over 7,000 years ago, with impossibly clear blue water.
places.tip: Open year-round, though snow can limit access to some areas outside summer.

places.name: Cannon Beach & Haystack Rock
places.description: The most iconic stop on the Oregon Coast — a massive sea stack visible (and walkable to at low tide) right off the beach.
places.tip: Time your visit around low tide for the closest approach to the rock.

places.name: Portland
places.description: A genuinely walkable, food-and-beer-obsessed city — 'Beervana' with 80-plus breweries, plus a serious coffee and food cart culture.
places.tip: The food cart pods are a better introduction to the city's food scene than any single restaurant.

places.name: Willamette Valley wine country
places.description: Internationally recognized Pinot Noir country, a short drive from Portland with tasting rooms ranging from casual to destination-worthy.
places.tip: The joint Pinot Noir Celebration draws wine lovers from well beyond Oregon.

places.name: Bandon
places.description: A quiet southern coast town with Face Rock's dramatic sea stacks and world-class golf at Bandon Dunes — genuinely under-visited relative to the northern coast.
places.tip: A good stop for travelers wanting the coast without Cannon Beach's crowds.

places.name: Ashland
places.description: Home to the internationally known Oregon Shakespeare Festival (February-November) — a genuine arts hub tucked into southern Oregon's mountains.
places.tip: Check the festival schedule ahead — performances are the reason to detour here.

places.name: Silver Falls State Park
places.description: A 'Trail of Ten Falls' loop hike passing behind several waterfalls — spectacular in fall foliage with morning fog adding to the atmosphere.
places.tip: Less crowded than the Columbia River Gorge waterfalls despite comparable scenery.

places.name: Lava Butte, Bend
places.description: A short, steep climb to an old fire lookout with sweeping Central Oregon views — a quick, high-reward stop most Bend visitors skip for the bigger-name trails.
places.tip: Pair with kayaking the Cascade Lakes nearby.

places.name: Portland craft beer ('Beervana')
places.description: Over 70 breweries in the metro area, with the state's proximity to hop fields making Oregon a center of 'fresh hop' beer made from hops picked within 24 hours.

places.name: Willamette Valley Pinot Noir
places.description: Internationally renowned wine country a short drive from Portland — one of the world's top Pinot Noir regions.

places.name: Voodoo Doughnut & Portland's donut culture
places.description: Serving over 100 wildly inventive donut varieties since 2003 — one of several beloved local shops locals rank alongside (or above) the famous one.

places.name: Food cart pods
places.description: Immigrant-owned food carts from Lao, Nordic, Latin American, and African traditions cluster in pods across Portland — arguably a more authentic food scene entry point than sit-down restaurants.

places.name: Third-wave coffee
places.description: Portland helped pioneer the third-wave coffee movement, with roasters like Stumptown originating here alongside a dense scene of independent shops.

name: Nevada
hero_tagline: Neon lights fifteen minutes from a 200,000-acre red rock desert most tourists never leave the Strip to see
hero_description: Las Vegas gets the headlines, but Red Rock Canyon, Lake Tahoe's Nevada shore, and a genuinely surprising Basque sheepherder culture in the north make this a far more layered state than the Strip suggests.
best_time_to_visit: Spring (March-May) for wildflowers and comfortable desert hiking temperatures, or fall (September-November) for the same reasons in reverse. Summer desert heat is severe — hiking Red Rock Canyon or the Mojave in July/August midday is genuinely dangerous.
altitude_or_climate_note: Southern Nevada (Las Vegas, Red Rock) is low desert with extreme summer heat; northern Nevada (Reno, Tahoe) sits at elevation with a cooler, four-season climate. Treat them as different trips.
permits_note: Red Rock Canyon requires a timed-entry vehicle reservation for the scenic drive during peak hours in high season — check current requirements before driving out.
gear_note: Carry more water than feels necessary for any desert hike, any season. Layers for northern Nevada's elevation swings, especially near Tahoe.

places.name: Red Rock Canyon Scenic Drive
places.description: A 13-mile one-way loop through nearly 200,000 acres of red sandstone peaks and canyons, just 15 miles from the Las Vegas Strip.
places.tip: Reservations may be required for the scenic drive in peak season — check current requirements ahead.

places.name: Turtlehead Peak Trail
places.description: A strenuous 5-mile hike gaining about 2,000 ft, with the single best panoramic view of Red Rock Canyon and the Las Vegas skyline beyond.
places.tip: Exposed for much of the route — avoid midday in summer entirely.

places.name: Ice Box Canyon Trail
places.description: A 2.2-mile hike into a canyon that stays cool even on hot days thanks to minimal sun exposure — best in spring when wildflowers are blooming.
places.tip: A good pick for a hot-weather visit when other trails feel too exposed.

places.name: Lake Tahoe, Nevada shore
places.description: The quieter, less-developed eastern shore of Tahoe, with the same brilliant blue water and mountain backdrop as the California side.
places.tip: Combine with a Reno base for a full Sierra Nevada experience.

places.name: Valley of Fire State Park
places.description: Nevada's oldest state park — vivid red Aztec sandstone formations, about an hour from Las Vegas and far less crowded than Red Rock Canyon.
places.tip: A good overflow option when Red Rock Canyon's reservations are full.

places.name: Great Basin National Park
places.description: One of the least-visited national parks in the country — ancient bristlecone pines, Lehman Caves, and some of the darkest night skies in the US.
places.tip: Genuinely remote — plan fuel and supplies carefully before heading out.

places.name: Las Vegas Strip
places.description: The casinos, shows, and neon that define Nevada's global image — a genuine spectacle regardless of whether you gamble.
places.tip: Old-school downtown Las Vegas (Fremont Street) offers a different, less polished energy than the modern Strip.

places.name: Hoover Dam & Lake Mead
places.description: An engineering landmark and the reservoir behind it, about 45 minutes from the Strip — a genuine change of pace from the casino floor.
places.tip: Guided tours go inside the dam itself, not just the exterior viewpoints.

places.name: Reno
places.description: Northern Nevada's hub — smaller and more relaxed than Las Vegas, with easy access to Lake Tahoe and a strong Basque-American food scene.
places.tip: A good base for exploring both Tahoe and northern Nevada's Basque restaurant circuit.

places.name: Winnemucca & Elko
places.description: Remote northern Nevada towns with deep Basque-American heritage — historic boarding-house restaurants still serve family-style Basque dinners.
places.tip: The Winnemucca Basque Festival (June) and National Basque Festival in Elko (July 4th weekend) are genuine cultural events, not tourist shows.

places.name: Cathedral Gorge State Park
places.description: Dramatic bentonite clay formations and narrow slot canyons in rural eastern Nevada — a genuine off-the-radar stop between Las Vegas and Great Basin.
places.tip: Combine with Valley of Fire or Great Basin for a longer eastern Nevada loop.

places.name: Downtown Las Vegas (Fremont Street)
places.description: The original Las Vegas casino district, grittier and more atmospheric than the modern Strip resorts.
places.tip: A good contrast stop if the Strip starts to feel like a theme park.

places.name: Calico Hills Trail
places.description: Combine with Turtlehead Peak for a longer, more strenuous Red Rock Canyon day involving genuine scrambling over colorful sandstone.
places.tip: Not for beginners — expect real scrambling, not just walking.

places.name: Basque sheepherder heritage
places.description: Basque immigrants arrived in northern Nevada in the mid-1800s as sheepherders; their boarding-house restaurants (ostatuak) still serve communal, family-style dinners in Reno, Elko, Winnemucca, and Gardnerville.

places.name: Picon Punch
places.description: Considered by many the unofficial state drink of Nevada — Torani Amer Picon, brandy, soda water, and grenadine, a Basque bar tradition since the 1800s.

places.name: Las Vegas buffet culture
places.description: Nearly every casino resort has its own all-you-can-eat buffet — a genuine Las Vegas institution distinct from the city's celebrity-chef fine dining scene.

places.name: Basque lamb dishes
places.description: Lamb is central to Basque-American cuisine, a direct legacy of the sheepherding industry — slow-roasted lamb shanks are a signature dish at historic Basque hotels like Winnemucca's Martin Hotel (since 1898).

name: Vermont
hero_tagline: The Green Mountain State delivers on the name, quaint villages and all
hero_description: Rolling hills, covered bridges, and world-class maple syrup — Vermont trades New Hampshire's rugged peaks for a gentler, more pastoral version of New England mountain country.
best_time_to_visit: Fall (late September-mid October) for iconic foliage along Route 100, or summer (June-August) for hiking and lake activities. Sugaring season (late winter, roughly February-April) is a distinctly Vermont experience worth timing around if maple syrup interests you.
altitude_or_climate_note: Peak foliage weekends bring serious traffic on scenic routes — book lodging well ahead and expect crowded overlooks.
permits_note: No special permits for most trails. Sugarhouses generally welcome walk-in visitors during sugaring season, though some request advance notice for tours.
gear_note: Sturdy footwear for Long Trail sections, which can be muddy. Layers for fall — mornings can be near-freezing even when afternoons are mild.

places.name: Camel's Hump
places.description: Vermont's third-highest peak and one of its most distinctive summits, visible from a great distance — a popular loop trail with exceptional fall foliage views.
places.tip: Peak fall weekends bring crowds — arrive early.

places.name: Route 100 & the Green Mountain Byway
places.description: Vermont's classic north-south scenic drive through the Green Mountains, passing Stowe and countless small towns.
places.tip: Time it for peak foliage in late September-early October.

places.name: Long Trail
places.description: America's oldest long-distance hiking trail, running the length of Vermont — day sections are accessible without committing to the full 272 miles.
places.tip: Shares its southern portion with the Appalachian Trail.

places.name: Mount Equinox summit drive
places.description: A 5-mile drive to a 360-degree summit view spanning the Green Mountains, White Mountains, Adirondacks, and Berkshires all at once.
places.tip: One of the few Vermont summits reachable by car, not just trail.

places.name: Shelburne Museum
places.description: A 45-acre open-air museum near Burlington with 39 historic structures blending art, architecture, and Americana.
places.tip: Plan at least half a day — it's far larger than a typical indoor museum visit.

places.name: Stowe
places.description: Vermont's best-known mountain town, with skiing in winter and hiking access in summer, anchored by Mount Mansfield, the state's highest peak.
places.tip: A good base for both Route 100 driving and Long Trail access.

places.name: Burlington
places.description: Vermont's largest city, on Lake Champlain, with a walkable downtown and easy access to the Shelburne Museum and lake activities.
places.tip: Church Street Marketplace is the natural walking hub downtown.

places.name: Sugarhouse tours
places.description: Working maple sugarhouses across the state welcome visitors during sugaring season (roughly February-April) to watch syrup production firsthand.
places.tip: Some request advance notice — call ahead during peak season.

places.name: Danville & Waterville
places.description: Small towns with some of the best under-visited fall foliage viewpoints in the state, overlooking both the Green and White Mountains.
places.tip: Quieter than the Stowe/Route 100 corridor during peak leaf season.

places.name: Covered bridges of Vermont
places.description: Vermont has more historic covered bridges per square mile than almost anywhere else in the country — many are unmarked finds off back roads.
places.tip: A good excuse for slow, aimless back-road driving between bigger destinations.

places.name: Maple syrup
places.description: A centuries-old Vermont tradition — the state produces some of the world's finest maple syrup, with sugarhouse tours and tastings during late-winter sugaring season.

places.name: Vermont cheddar & farmstead cheese
places.description: A strong dairy and artisan cheese tradition, with farmstead creameries scattered across the state's rural roads.

places.name: Craft beer
places.description: Vermont punches well above its size in craft brewing, with a dense concentration of small breweries relative to population.

places.name: Farm-to-table & general store culture
places.description: Vermont's small-town general stores and farm stands anchor a food culture built around local, seasonal ingredients rather than chain dining.

name: New Hampshire
hero_tagline: 1,200 miles of trail and the highest peak in the Northeast
hero_description: The White Mountains are a genuine hiker's paradise, with Mount Washington's notoriously extreme summit weather as the crown jewel — plus one of the most celebrated scenic drives in the country.
best_time_to_visit: Late September-mid October for peak foliage along the Kancamagus Highway, or summer (June-August) for full trail access. Late spring (before summer rush) offers more solitude but check trail reports — snow can linger.
altitude_or_climate_note: Mount Washington has some of the most extreme and unpredictable weather in North America, regardless of season — check the summit forecast separately from the valley forecast before any attempt.
permits_note: No general park permits required for most White Mountain trails. Franconia Notch parking fills early in peak season.
gear_note: Microspikes are worth carrying even in late spring on higher trails, where snow and ice can linger. Layers are essential for any Mount Washington attempt regardless of valley conditions.

places.name: Franconia Ridge Loop
places.description: One of the most celebrated hikes in the Northeast — an exposed ridgeline walk connecting multiple 4,000-footers with sweeping White Mountains views.
places.tip: A strenuous full-day hike — start early and check weather carefully given the exposed ridge.

places.name: Kancamagus Highway
places.description: A 34-mile scenic byway through the White Mountains, considered one of the most beautiful drives in the country, especially during fall foliage.
places.tip: Numerous pullouts and short trails branch off — budget extra time beyond just the drive.

places.name: Mount Washington
places.description: At 6,288 ft, the highest peak in the Northeast, notorious for hosting some of the most extreme recorded weather on Earth — reachable by hiking, driving, or the historic Cog Railway.
places.tip: The Cog Railway (over 150 years old) is a good option for reaching the summit without the hike.

places.name: Carter Notch Loop
places.description: A rigorous 10-mile loop over Mount Hight and Carter Dome, passing through a dramatic mountain pass with two mirrored lakes and a secluded AMC hut.
places.tip: The Appalachian Mountain Club hut serves soup and snacks — a nice reward mid-hike.

places.name: White Mountain National Forest
places.description: Over 1,200 miles of trails across a forest covering roughly a quarter of the state — the anchor of New Hampshire's outdoor reputation.
places.tip: Fall foliage weekends bring the heaviest crowds and traffic.

places.name: Lake Winnipesaukee
places.description: New Hampshire's largest lake, ringed by charming small towns — boating, fishing, and lakeside exploring.
places.tip: A good lower-key complement to a mountain-focused White Mountains trip.

places.name: Cannon Mountain
places.description: A well-regarded ski resort in winter, with an aerial tramway offering summit access and views year-round.
places.tip: The tramway is a good no-hike option for Franconia Notch views.

places.name: Late spring hiking window
places.description: Before the summer rush begins, White Mountain trails offer real solitude — locals recommend this window specifically for avoiding crowds.
places.tip: Bring microspikes — snow and ice can linger on higher trails even as valleys warm up.

places.name: Small lakeside towns off Winnipesaukee
places.description: Away from the lake's busier resort areas, smaller lakeside communities offer a quieter version of the same scenery.
places.tip: Worth exploring by car along the lake's back roads.

places.name: New England clam chowder
places.description: A cream-based chowder tradition shared across the region, found in diners and seafood shacks throughout the state.

places.name: Maple syrup
places.description: Like its Vermont neighbor, New Hampshire has a genuine maple sugaring tradition, with farm tours available in late winter.

places.name: Colonial and mountain-town heritage
places.description: New Hampshire's identity blends colonial New England history with a mountain-town, outdoor-recreation culture distinct from its coastal neighbors.

name: Massachusetts
hero_tagline: Walk the Revolution in the morning, hike the Berkshires by afternoon
hero_description: Boston's colonial history and college-town energy, Cape Cod's 550 miles of coastline, and the Berkshires' mountains and arts scene make this a genuinely compact state with an outsized range of experiences.
best_time_to_visit: Fall (September-October) for Berkshires foliage and pleasant hiking weather — peak foliage hits the Berkshires in early October, the coast by late October. Late spring (April-May) is best for Boston with fewer crowds; shoulder-season Cape Cod (May or September) is significantly cheaper with still-warm water.
altitude_or_climate_note: A car in Boston itself is often more liability than asset — the subway (the 'T') covers the city well. You'll want a car for the Berkshires and Cape Cod.
permits_note: No special permits needed for most attractions; the CapeFLYER seasonal train and ferries to Martha's Vineyard/Nantucket run on limited schedules — check ahead.
gear_note: Comfortable walking shoes for Boston's Freedom Trail and cobblestone neighborhoods. Layers for Berkshires hiking, where mountain weather shifts faster than the coast.

places.name: Mount Greylock
places.description: The highest point in Massachusetts, in the Berkshires — a genuine mountain-hiking experience that surprises visitors who think of the state as purely coastal and colonial.
places.tip: Combine with a Bash Bish Falls stop nearby for a full Berkshires nature day.

places.name: Mohawk Trail Scenic Byway
places.description: A historic scenic route through the Berkshires, especially striking during fall foliage.
places.tip: Time it for early October when Berkshires foliage typically peaks.

places.name: Cape Cod National Seashore dunes
places.description: Windswept dunes and the Pilgrim Monument in Provincetown, with panoramic harbor views from the monument's top.
places.tip: Parking in Provincetown proper can be genuinely difficult — plan ahead.

places.name: Whale watching, Cape Cod
places.description: Regular whale sightings on guided tours departing from Cape Cod ports — a genuine wildlife experience, not just a boat ride.
places.tip: Summer offers the most reliable sightings.

places.name: Freedom Trail, Boston
places.description: A 2.5-mile walking route through 16 historically significant Revolutionary War sites, threading Beacon Hill and the North End.
places.tip: Patriots' Day (April) is considered by many the single best day to walk it.

places.name: Cape Cod beach towns
places.description: 15 distinct towns along 70 miles of coastline between the Cape Cod Canal and Provincetown, each with its own beach character.
places.tip: The Cape quiets down considerably in fall — a cozier, less crowded experience.

places.name: Martha's Vineyard & Nantucket
places.description: Island getaways off Cape Cod, reachable by ferry, both known for beaches, bluffs, and historic whaling-town character.
places.tip: Easy day trips or overnight adds from the Cape.

places.name: Salem
places.description: Famous for the 1692 witch trials, but also a genuine maritime history hub with the Peabody Essex Museum — worth visiting beyond just Halloween season.
places.tip: Far less crowded outside October, with the maritime history still fully accessible.

places.name: Gloucester & Rockport
places.description: Charming fishing villages on Cape Ann, north of Boston, with Halibut Point State Park's coastal views and a quieter alternative to Cape Cod.
places.tip: A good day trip from Boston without the Cape's summer crowds.

places.name: MASS MoCA
places.description: A contemporary art museum in a converted North Adams factory — one of the largest contemporary art spaces in the country, tucked into the Berkshires.
places.tip: Pair with Mount Greylock for an art-and-hiking Berkshires day.

places.name: Tanglewood
places.description: The Boston Symphony Orchestra's summer home in Lenox — outdoor concerts on the lawn are a genuine Berkshires summer tradition.
places.tip: Bring a picnic and blanket for lawn seating, the classic way to experience it.

places.name: Norman Rockwell Museum
places.description: A museum dedicated to the iconic American illustrator, in the small Berkshires town of Stockbridge that inspired much of his work.
places.tip: Combine with Tanglewood and Mount Greylock for a full Berkshires day.

places.name: Lobster roll & clam chowder
places.description: Massachusetts' seafood identity, from Cape Cod shacks to Boston restaurants — creamy New England-style chowder and simply-dressed lobster rolls.

places.name: College-town energy
places.description: Harvard, MIT, Williams, and Smith anchor a youthful, intellectual culture that shapes everything from Cambridge's bookshops to the Berkshires' arts scene.

places.name: Colonial & Revolutionary heritage
places.description: Boston, Lexington, and Concord anchor the birthplace-of-the-Revolution identity that runs through the state's historic sites and Patriots' Day traditions.

places.name: Fenway Park & Red Sox culture
places.description: Baseball is closer to civic religion than sport in Boston — a game at Fenway is as much cultural experience as entertainment.

name: Rhode Island
hero_tagline: The smallest state, 400 miles of shoreline, and a beach house that once belonged to Taylor Swift
hero_description: Newport's Gilded Age mansions and Cliff Walk anchor 'America's First Resort,' while Providence's Little Italy and Block Island's quiet bluffs round out a state small enough to see most of in a long weekend.
best_time_to_visit: June through early September for warm, swimmable beaches. Fall brings quieter towns and comfortable hiking weather on Block Island and along the coastal trails.
altitude_or_climate_note: Being the smallest state works in your favor — most destinations are under an hour apart, so weather rarely forces a change of plans for the whole trip.
permits_note: Block Island requires a ferry — check the seasonal schedule, which is more limited outside summer. The Newport-Providence ferry also runs seasonally only.
gear_note: Good walking shoes for the Cliff Walk's 3.5-mile coastal path. Beach gear for Block Island and South County's quieter beaches.

places.name: Newport Cliff Walk
places.description: A 3.5-mile coastal path past Gilded Age mansions on one side and crashing Atlantic surf on the other — regularly called one of the most romantic walks in New England.
places.tip: Start early to see the mansions and coastline before crowds build.

places.name: Mohegan Bluffs, Block Island
places.description: Dramatic 150-ft clay cliffs on Block Island, with a steep staircase down to the beach below.
places.tip: Combine with the historic Southeast Lighthouse nearby.

places.name: Block Island
places.description: A peaceful island getaway reachable by ferry, with hiking trails, quiet beaches, and a genuinely slower pace than the mainland.
places.tip: Ferry schedules are more limited outside summer — check ahead.

places.name: Neutaconkanut Hill, Providence
places.description: An 88-acre urban wilderness park with stone walls, glacial boulders, and wildflowers — genuine hiking within Providence's city limits.
places.tip: A good surprise stop for anyone assuming Rhode Island's capital is all city.

places.name: The Breakers & Newport mansions
places.description: The grandest of Newport's Gilded Age 'summer cottages,' open to the public for tours into 19th-century elite life.
places.tip: Several mansions offer combo tickets — worth it if visiting more than one.

places.name: Providence's Federal Hill
places.description: Providence's Little Italy — Italian restaurants, DePasquale Square, and the city's famous WaterFire art installation nearby.
places.tip: Check the WaterFire schedule — it doesn't run year-round.

places.name: Mystic Seaport (Connecticut border)
places.description: A recreated 19th-century seafaring village and living history museum just over the Connecticut line, an easy day trip from Newport.
places.tip: Good for families — hands-on demonstrations from coopers and blacksmiths.

places.name: Watch Hill
places.description: A quiet, upscale beach town with grand 'cottages' and a pretty harbor — less crowded than Newport with a similar coastal charm.
places.tip: Good sunset spot away from the bigger crowds.

places.name: Wuskenau Beach
places.description: A smaller, quieter alternative to nearby Misquamicut State Beach, with soft sand and fewer crowds.
places.tip: Free parking is limited — arrive early in summer.

places.name: Beavertail State Park
places.description: Dramatic rocky coastline and a historic lighthouse on Jamestown, with far fewer visitors than Newport just across the bridge.
places.tip: A good sunset spot with wide-open ocean views.

places.name: Stuffies
places.description: A quahog clam filled with chopped clams, breadcrumbs, and herbs — a Rhode Island specialty found nowhere else quite like it.

places.name: Coffee milk
places.description: Rhode Island's official state drink — milk flavored with coffee syrup, a local institution predating today's coffee culture.

places.name: Grilled pizza & clam cakes
places.description: Providence-style grilled pizza (invented at Il Forno in 1980) and clam cakes, distinct from crab cakes, are local specialties worth seeking out.

places.name: Sailing culture
places.description: Newport and Jamestown are genuine sailing hubs, not just tourist marinas — the America's Cup was raced from Newport for decades.

name: Connecticut
hero_tagline: Wooden whaleships, a wine trail, and the pizza that started an interstate rivalry
hero_description: Mystic's seafaring history, the Litchfield Hills' posh farm country, and a fiercely defended apizza tradition make Connecticut more than just the drive between New York and Boston.
best_time_to_visit: Fall (late September-October) for foliage in the Litchfield Hills and along the Connecticut Wine Trail, or summer for coastal towns and Long Island Sound beaches.
altitude_or_climate_note: The state splits cleanly between a developed southern coast (New Haven, Mystic) and quieter, hillier northwest countryside (Litchfield Hills, Taconic range) — decide which experience you want before planning a route.
permits_note: No special permits for most attractions; Mystic Seaport and similar living-history sites have their own posted hours worth checking ahead.
gear_note: Comfortable shoes for exploring Mystic's walkable downtown. Layers for Litchfield Hills and Taconic range hiking in cooler months.

places.name: Taconic Range hikes
places.description: Ranges from easy to moderately difficult trails in Connecticut's northwest corner, with genuinely photogenic mountain scenery most visitors don't associate with the state.
places.tip: Pair with a Litchfield Hills farm-country drive.

places.name: Connecticut Wine Trail
places.description: A scenic drive through the state's vineyards, offering tastings alongside genuinely rural New England countryside.
places.tip: A relaxed alternative to the busier coastal towns.

places.name: Litchfield Hills farm country
places.description: Posh, rolling countryside in Connecticut's northwest corner — a quieter, more pastoral side of the state.
places.tip: Good for a slow driving day with no fixed itinerary.

places.name: Mystic Seaport
places.description: A recreated 19th-century seafaring village and living history museum, with the Charles W. Morgan — the world's last surviving wooden whaleship — on display.
places.tip: A strong pick for families with kids interested in hands-on history.

places.name: Mystic downtown
places.description: A walkable historic district with the movie-famous Mystic Pizza, boutiques, and a drawbridge over the harbor.
places.tip: Grab ice cream and watch boats pass under the lifted drawbridge.

places.name: Salisbury & the Taconic range
places.description: A quiet northwest-corner town anchoring some of the state's best under-visited hiking, far from the coastal tourist circuit.
places.tip: A genuine off-the-radar stop for hikers who assume Connecticut is only suburbs.

places.name: New Haven apizza
places.description: Thin-crust, coal-fired pizza with a devoted local following — New Haven's apizza scene (Frank Pepe's, Sally's) is a genuine point of regional pride.

places.name: New England clam chowder & lobster rolls
places.description: Shared with the rest of the region — Connecticut's shoreline towns serve the same creamy chowder and simply-dressed lobster rolls found across New England.

places.name: Connecticut wine country
places.description: A genuine, if under-the-radar, wine region in the state's rural northwest, with tasting rooms along the dedicated Wine Trail.

name: Pennsylvania
hero_tagline: Amish farmland, coal-mining history, and a cheesesteak rivalry that never really ends
hero_description: Philadelphia's Revolutionary landmarks, Lancaster County's genuinely lived-in Amish communities, and the Poconos' underrated hiking make Pennsylvania a lot more than the turnpike drive between New York and Ohio.
best_time_to_visit: Fall (September-October) for Poconos foliage and comfortable hiking weather, or spring (April-May) for Philadelphia and Lancaster County without summer humidity.
altitude_or_climate_note: The Poconos, Lancaster's farm country, and Philadelphia/Pittsburgh's cities each have distinct characters — plan realistic drive times between them rather than trying to combine all three in a short trip.
permits_note: No special permits for most attractions. Amish Country tours are best booked through a respectful, established operator (Amish Farm & House, Amish Experience) rather than approaching Amish families directly.
gear_note: Sturdy footwear for Lancaster Conservancy trails like Kellys Run, which involve real stream crossings and scrambling despite the county's flat-farmland reputation.

places.name: Kellys Run
places.description: A demanding 3.8-mile loop through a hemlock-shaded gorge in Lancaster County — stream crossings and bedrock scrambles most visitors don't expect from 'flat farmland' terrain.
places.tip: Hike-in only, no facilities beyond a portable toilet — come prepared.

places.name: Pocono Mountains
places.description: A year-round outdoor playground for hiking, biking, skiing, and kayaking, with 18-waterfall hikes and old-growth pine forest.
places.tip: The region also holds real coal-mining and Gilded Age history alongside the outdoor recreation.

places.name: Lackawanna Coal Mine Tour
places.description: Descend 1,600 feet into the longest continuously operated deep mine in the world — genuine industrial history, not a recreation.
places.tip: Dress warmly — it's cool underground regardless of the season above.

places.name: Appalachian Trail (Pennsylvania section)
places.description: The trail runs through the state for hikers wanting a taste of the AT without a full thru-hike commitment.
places.tip: Pair a day section with a stop in a nearby trail town.

places.name: Independence Hall & the Liberty Bell
places.description: Philadelphia's Revolutionary War landmarks, alongside Elfreth's Alley — a deep, walkable dive into American independence history.
places.tip: Free timed tickets for Independence Hall are worth reserving ahead in peak season.

places.name: Lancaster County Amish Country
places.description: One of the most immersive views into Amish culture in the US — horse-drawn buggies, farmland, and roadside stands across Bird-in-Hand, Intercourse, and Strasburg.
places.tip: Visit respectfully through an established tour operator rather than approaching Amish families directly.

places.name: Gettysburg National Military Park
places.description: The site of the Civil War's turning-point battle, with guided tours and a genuinely moving battlefield walk.
places.tip: A licensed battlefield guide adds significant context beyond a self-guided drive.

places.name: Hershey
places.description: The 'Sweetest Place on Earth' — the Hershey chocolate factory experience anchors a whole town built around it.
places.tip: Pair with nearby Lancaster for a full Central Pennsylvania day.

places.name: Longwood Gardens
places.description: Over 1,100 acres of formal gardens, fountains, and grand greenhouses under an hour from Philadelphia — far less crowded than the city's core attractions.
places.tip: A good half-day counterpoint to Philadelphia's historic sites.

places.name: Lititz
places.description: A small town just north of Lancaster with the Roots Country Market — a genuine local farmers market most tourists never find.
places.tip: Go early on a Tuesday for the market's best selection.

places.name: Bedford County
places.description: A destination for travelers who want to go beyond the standard Pennsylvania circuit — local culture and outdoor adventure with far fewer crowds.
places.tip: A good detour for travelers who've already done Lancaster and the Poconos.

places.name: Philly cheesesteak
places.description: Philadelphia's signature sandwich, with a passionately defended local rivalry over the 'right' way to order it (Pat's vs. Geno's is the classic debate).

places.name: Pennsylvania Dutch cooking
places.description: Scrapple, shoofly pie, and whoopie pies reflect the Pennsylvania Dutch (Amish and Mennonite) culinary tradition centered on Lancaster County.

places.name: Pierogies & Primanti sandwiches
places.description: Pittsburgh's Eastern European immigrant heritage shows up in beloved pierogi shops, alongside the city's own Primanti Bros. sandwich piled with fries right inside the bread.

places.name: Amish craftsmanship
places.description: Handmade quilts, furniture, baskets, and leather goods reflect a living tradition of craftsmanship still practiced by hand in Lancaster County.

name: New Jersey
hero_tagline: 1.1 million acres of pine forest most people driving I-95 have no idea is there
hero_description: Past the turnpike stereotype: a genuine wilderness in the Pine Barrens, Victorian charm in Cape May, and 130 miles of shore towns most visitors never look past the beach traffic to find.
best_time_to_visit: Spring (May-early June) and fall (September-October) for culture, history, and hiking with milder temperatures. Summer is peak shore season — expect serious Parkway traffic on weekends.
altitude_or_climate_note: The Pine Barrens (south/central) and the Kittatinny Mountains/Delaware Water Gap (north) offer genuinely different terrain within the same small state — don't assume 'New Jersey' means flat or coastal everywhere.
permits_note: No general permits for Pine Barrens hiking; Island Beach State Park and other shore parks charge a seasonal vehicle fee.
gear_note: Layers for Mount Tammany and Kittatinny ridge hikes, which involve real elevation gain despite the state's low-key reputation. Standard beach gear for the shore.

places.name: Mount Tammany, Delaware Water Gap
places.description: A 3-mile roundtrip climbing 1,200-1,500 ft to a spectacular view over the Delaware Water Gap, especially striking in fall foliage.
places.tip: The Red Dot Trail is the steeper, more direct route; the Blue Blaze Trail is gentler.

places.name: Pine Barrens
places.description: 1.1 million acres of forest and freshwater aquifers covering about 22% of the state's land — hiking, canoeing, and the local Jersey Devil folklore all in one place.
places.tip: The Pine Barrens Scenic Byway is a good way to sample the region by car first.

places.name: Island Beach State Park
places.description: A rugged, undeveloped 10-mile barrier island between the Atlantic and Barnegat Bay, with 3,000 acres of dunes and the state's largest osprey colony.
places.tip: A genuine wild-beach contrast to the developed shore towns nearby.

places.name: High Point State Park
places.description: New Jersey's highest point at 1,803 ft, with views spanning three states from the summit monument.
places.tip: A good stop combined with a broader Kittatinny Ridge day.

places.name: Cape May
places.description: One of the country's oldest seaside resorts, known for preserved Victorian architecture, walkable streets, and a developed food and wine scene.
places.tip: Stays lively past Labor Day with fall Victorian-themed events.

places.name: Jersey Shore boardwalks
places.description: 130 miles of coastline and the boardwalk culture that defines the state's summer identity — 'down the shore' to locals.
places.tip: Expect serious traffic on the Parkway during summer weekends.

places.name: Great Falls of Paterson
places.description: One of the largest waterfalls on the East Coast, tied to early American industrial history and now a National Historical Park.
places.tip: An easy, quick stop with viewing platforms right off the walking trails.

places.name: Franklin Parker Preserve
places.description: At 16 square miles, the largest New Jersey Conservation Foundation property in the Pine Barrens — genuine solitude for hiking and birdwatching.
places.tip: Far less visited than the more accessible Pine Barrens trailheads.

places.name: Double Trouble State Park
places.description: A quieter Pine Barrens hiking spot with multi-use trails through cedar forest and old cranberry bogs.
places.tip: Shared with bikers and horseback riders — a genuinely local, uncrowded trail network.

places.name: Hoboken
places.description: Frank Sinatra's birthplace, with Manhattan skyline views across the Hudson and a food scene that punches above its size.
places.tip: A good day trip that pairs New York City views with genuinely good pizza.

places.name: Jersey tomatoes & farm stands
places.description: The Garden State earns its nickname — summer tomatoes from Jersey farm stands are a genuine point of local pride.

places.name: Pork roll (or Taylor ham)
places.description: A breakfast sandwich staple whose very name sparks a serious regional debate — North Jersey says 'Taylor ham,' South Jersey says 'pork roll.'

places.name: Diner culture
places.description: New Jersey has more diners per capita than anywhere else in the country — a genuine 24-hour institution, not just a nostalgia trip.

places.name: Jersey Devil folklore
places.description: A local legend tied to the Pine Barrens that adds genuine regional mystery and identity to the forest's reputation.

name: Virginia
hero_tagline: Mountains meet the sea, with a Chesapeake island where locals still speak a dialect close to original English settlers
hero_description: Shenandoah's 105-mile Skyline Drive, colonial history dating to the country's founding, and a genuinely surprising wine and craft beer scene make Virginia one of the most complete single-state trips on the East Coast.
best_time_to_visit: Early-to-mid October for peak Blue Ridge foliage along Skyline Drive, or spring (April-May) for wildflowers and milder hiking weather with fewer crowds.
altitude_or_climate_note: Shenandoah Valley sits between the Blue Ridge and Allegheny mountains and runs noticeably cooler than the Chesapeake Bay coast — pack for both if combining a mountain-and-coast itinerary.
permits_note: Shenandoah National Park charges a per-vehicle entrance fee (around $30). Check the park website for closures before visiting — sections occasionally close for weather or maintenance.
gear_note: Sturdy footwear for Old Rag Mountain, which involves genuine rock scrambling, not just walking. Layers for Blue Ridge elevation changes.

places.name: Skyline Drive, Shenandoah
places.description: A 105-mile scenic highway along the crest of the Blue Ridge Mountains, with numerous overlooks and access to backcountry trails.
places.tip: Early fall brings peak foliage but also peak crowds — weekday visits are noticeably quieter.

places.name: Old Rag Mountain
places.description: Shenandoah's most famous hike — a genuine rock scramble to a summit with 360-degree Blue Ridge views.
